r.x: Gutta-percha and Redmanol

are two materials that were tried in pipe mouthpiece (stem) making and have since both been abandoned. There's no chemical kinship between them: one is a plant-derived thermoplastic drawn from Southeast Asian trees, the other an early product of the American plastics industry, a synthetic resin. What they share is that both were put forward as replacements for amber and hardened rubber, and neither one lasted. Both appear mostly in pipes with briar bowls, as well as in cigar and cigarette holders.
What Gutta-Percha Is
Gutta-percha is obtained by refining and coagulating the latex of trees of the genus
Palaquium

, in the family Sapotaceae; the name comes from Malay. It softens when heated and hardens on cooling, holding the shape it's given; unlike rubber, it doesn't spring back. Being moldable made it a sought-after raw material in 19th-century industry. Insulation for submarine telegraph cables, root-canal fillings in dentistry, and golf balls known as "gutties" are its best-known uses.

The first person in Europe to study the material was John Tradescant, who brought a sample from the Far East in 1656 and named it "mazer wood." Practical use came two centuries later, and after the physician William Montgomerie, serving in British India, recognized the material's medical value, the Royal Society of Arts awarded him a gold medal in 1843.
Gutta-Percha in the Mouthpiece

Exactly when the material entered pipe making is not documented. According to English patent abstracts, an 1860 application (Joseph Jobin and Auguste Boll) proposes using vulcanized rubber or gutta-percha at the tip end of the mouthpiece. Another application from 1868 (Lorkin) describes a spiral tube that cools the smoke along its length, ending in a gutta-percha tip; the rationale given is that hard materials like amber and bone wear down the teeth. Tobacco pouches were also made of gutta-percha in the same years.

Even so, the material never gained standing as a mouthpiece. A recurring complaint in period writing is that it spoiled the taste of the tobacco. Because its appearance closely resembled hardened rubber, it was recommended that the two be told apart by checking whether it left a salty taste in the mouth. Once vulcanite and ebonite became widespread, gutta-percha was pushed out of the mouthpiece.
The Search for Amber, and Redmanol

At the start of the century, the most prized mouthpiece material was amber; but it was an expensive import and broke easily. The first substitute was bakelite, developed by Leo Hendrik Baekeland in Yonkers, New York, in 1907, with the patent granted in 1909: the first fully synthetic resin, produced from the reaction of phenol with formaldehyde, and one that couldn't be reshaped by heat once set. Cast bakelite was worked as "artificial amber" into mouthpieces, cigarette holders, and jewelry.

Redmanol is the second contender for the same market. Canadian chemist Lawrence V. Redman (1880-1946) founded the Redmanol Chemical Products Company in 1913 with the backing of Chicago furniture manufacturer S. Karpen & Bros. According to a 1926 chemistry journal article, Redmanol was produced using formin instead of formaldehyde, yielding a clear, amber-colored, semi-translucent mass; its appeal in a mouthpiece came from this translucency. Records show M. Linkman & Co. and Reiss Bros. (Chicago), S. M. Frank & Co. and L. & H. Stern (New York), and Premier Briar Pipe Co. (New Jersey) among the manufacturers using Redmanol mouthpieces starting in 1919; it's also noted that Peterson used it on some of its briar models.
The Two Names Blur, and the End

Following patent suits that were decided in Baekeland's favor, General Bakelite, Condensite, and Redmanol merged in 1922 under the Bakelite Corporation umbrella; Redman became vice president and director of research at the new company. Production continued, but because the two names were advertised side by side, collectors today have trouble telling red bakelite apart from Redmanol. The trade press of the period objected to this marketing language, writing that phenol-based amber imitations lost their color under light. Records indicate both materials fell out of favor in the period stretching from the late 1930s to the early 1940s; brittleness, along with the cost and difficulty of production, are cited as the main reasons. The materials used in mouthpieces today are covered in the article on mouthpiece materials.

r.x: Making pipes from morta

differs from making them from briar most of all in where and how the raw material comes from. Briar blocks can be ordered already cut, sorted, and dried; morta, on the other hand, is a trunk that small crews dig out of a bog by hand, that must be rested for years, and most of which is lost to waste. This trio of bottlenecks — limited extraction permits, long drying, and high wastage — has kept morta pipe-making a small-scale field that relies almost entirely on hand labor.
Extraction from the Bog

The morta source most often cited in pipe-making is the Brière bog in France's Loire-Atlantique region. The roughly seven-thousand-hectare area known as the Grande Brière Mottière is held in common by twenty-one communes; a syndicate commission established in 1838, together with the Brière Regional Nature Park, sets who may extract how much and on what dates through annual agreements. Because water only recedes in autumn, the window is narrow: under current rules, September 15 to October 30 — close to six weeks a year. No heavy machinery is allowed on the site. Prospectors probe the ground by driving a long metal skewer into the peat; when the skewer strikes a solid mass, the spot is marked, and the trunk's boundaries are traced through successive probing. Extraction is done with a shovel and spade, the trunk is cut into portable pieces, and the pit is refilled and its top layer replaced the same day. Records note trunks found at depths exceeding a meter. Only ten to twenty percent of the wood extracted turns out to be workable.
Drying and Sorting

Morta releases moisture faster than briar; a trunk left exposed dries quickly on the outside and develops deep cracks. This is why logs are kept in closed, dark storage, their cut faces sealed, and moisture removed slowly; kiln drying is not used. Sources don't agree on how long to wait: the lower limit most often cited is two years, and thick logs are reported to take three to four years to reach a moisture level suitable for pipe-making. Once the wait is over, the trunk is first cut into cross-sections, then into blocks on a band saw. This is where the real sorting happens; every cut surface reveals new cracks and rotted areas, and blocks are taken only from the parts that remain sound. Morta doesn't show briar's sand pits; flaws appear instead as fine cracks and degraded wood. Because rings mark the tree's annual growth, a block can also be oriented for the desired ring density.
The Shape the Material Dictates

Morta blocks are mostly shorter and more square in proportion than briar blocks. This is a limit that directly narrows the shape repertoire: the shank stays short, the margin between the tenon and the tobacco chamber thins out, and drilling becomes a millimeter-precise task. Shank extensions made with materials like bamboo are the known solution to this squeeze. The material doesn't turn as cleanly on a lathe as briar does — it tends to chip at the edges; at the Talbert workshop, it's said that shaping the body by hand on a sanding disc gives better results than finishing it on the lathe. Bits and small reamers made for metal rather than wood perform better on morta. Friction heats the material up quickly and also dulls the abrasive surface fast, so pressing the disc for long stretches is avoided. The general stages of making a pipe stay the same, but at every step the surface is checked with a magnifier for hidden cracks.
Finishing and Stamping

Morta doesn't take stain; the color is in the wood itself, and finishing is a shorter sequence of steps than with briar. On the other hand, the porous surface pulls in polishing compound, and cleaning requires a fine-bristled brush; most makers settle for oil and beeswax rather than heavy buffing. The surface is generally sanded up to grit 600; going to finer papers gives limited returns — morta doesn't hold the high gloss briar does, and settles into a satin look with use. Stem work can be split by tier; at the Talbert workshop, ready-cast stems are thinned and adapted for the Classic tier, while for the Signature tier the stem is cut entirely by hand. In both cases the stem's bore is matched to the shank's hole, and the button's interior is opened wide enough for a pipe cleaner to pass through. The last step is the stamp; that fine lettering doesn't come out legibly on the porous surface is a difficulty Talbert has voiced regarding morta pipes.

r.x: Sandblasting

is the process of driving abrasive particles against a surface using compressed air. It was not invented for pipes: Benjamin Chew Tilghman's American patent (No. 108408) of 18 October 1870 aimed to cut, engrave, and clean stone, glass, and metal. Its application to wood — let alone a pipe stummel — took roughly half a century longer; once it arrived, it stopped being a mere cleaning method and became a craft with its own standards.
Why a Stummel Gets Sandblasted

The first reasons are practical. If a block has a sand mark, a fine crack, or an unevenly staining color patch, blasting the surface is a faster fix than reworking the stummel; because the process removes material from the wood, it also trims a bit of weight from the finished pipe. The resulting judgment that "a sandblasted pipe is a flawed pipe" is considered too sweeping; sandblasting has long stood as a finishing choice in its own right.
The Dunhill Patent and the Priority Debate

The figure who made sandblasting a classic in pipe making is Alfred Dunhill. Records credit the first batch of Algerian briar he bought in 1914 — after opening his tobacconist's shop on Duke Street in London's St James's in 1907 — with causing trouble on a smooth surface because of its softness, and thereby setting off the search. The British patent for the process was granted in 1918, its American counterpart in 1920.

What the patent protects isn't the blasting itself but the preparation that accompanies it. Per the specification, briar is soaked in mineral or vegetable oil for weeks, then left under heat for days, with the oil seeping to the surface skimmed off regularly; only after this is the blasting done, the cycle repeated until the desired relief appears. The rationale is durability, not decoration: wood that hasn't been oil-treated is said to be prone to cracking during blasting. The popular narrative crediting Dunhill as the first maker to use sandblasting in pipes is disputed; one independently unverified researcher's view points to the Barling "Niblick" model, dated to mid-1917, as a possible precursor.
Abrasive and Machine

The first variable shaping the result is the type of grain. Silica sand, glass beads, steel shot, garnet, and ground walnut shell are all common options; since their hardness and grain shape differ, each leaves a different texture. It's routine for a material that gives the desired look in one workshop to fail to reproduce that same result in another.

The second variable is the machine setup. In a suction (vacuum) setup, compressed air creates suction inside the gun that draws the abrasive in; since pressure is limited to roughly one atmosphere, it doesn't produce deep texture. In a pressure setup, the abrasive is held under air pressure inside a sealed vessel; the flow is far more forceful, and pressure is adjustable. Workshops known for deep, sharp sandblasts, such as Ashton, are known to work with this second setup.

In mass production there's a third route: stummels are loaded into a wire drum, and a fixed nozzle blasts for hours while the drum turns. Because the pieces rub against each other and pressure is kept relatively low, edges round off. A sandblasted stummel with distinct, sharp edges is taken as a sign of hand work; soft, rounded ones point to the drum.
Wood, Cut, and Curing

The underlying wood also shapes the result. It's accepted that the softness of Algerian briar gave early sandblasts extra depth, and that surfaces from later generations grew shallower once this source dried up after the 1960s; this view rests on collector observation rather than measurement. How the block is cut matters too: blocks cut for straight grain give a ring-patterned surface when blasted, while cross-grained blocks give a more variable pattern. Makers don't agree on curing method (air-drying, kiln-drying, oil curing, steaming); some workshops argue their method improves the result directly, while others report seeing no meaningful difference.

Sandblasting therefore can't be reduced to a recipe. The same machine, same pressure, and same abrasive can give two different surfaces on two different blocks; which combination works is workshop-specific and is learned largely through trial. That's also why craft is the most debated aspect among the surface finishes, with sandblasting at the center of it.

r.x: Meerschaum in literature

is a rarely discussed but surprisingly wide branch of pipe history. Meerschaum in the 19th century wasn't only a bowl material; it was also the subject of essayists, poets, and painters. According to compilations surveying the period's printed record, the number of poems and essays devoted to the material exceeds what was written about briar, which came to dominate the market in the second half of the same century; briar's own literature, by contrast, remained largely confined to trade, technical, and historical subjects.
Guides Devoted to Coloring

The first cluster of texts grew directly out of the craft. That meerschaum turned from creamy white to amber and then to deep brown with use was a process that fascinated the era's reader, and small booklets were printed devoted purely to this process. Records mention, among these, a twelve-rule coloring guide published under the signature of an "old smoker," and
Meerschaums and How to Colour Them

, published in London in 1871 under the pen name "Amator Fumi." Today these publications read like a kind of user manual; for the pipe owner of the period, they were a handbook for a pursuit that demanded patience.
A Favorite of Poetry
The earliest known standalone book of pipe poetry is considered to be Isaac Hawkins Browne's 1736 London collection of parody verse,
A Pipe of Tobacco
. The genre spread in the 19th century; Joseph Knight's 1894 compilation
Pipe and Pouch
gathered poems on pipes and tobacco into a single volume. This and similar anthologies are covered further in the article on pipe books and publications.
There are also examples devoted directly to meerschaum. Rudyard Kipling included a Swinburne parody titled "The Maid of the Meerschaum" in
Echoes
, printed in Lahore in July 1884; the poem is built on the idea of a young girl figure carved into a bowl losing her whiteness as she's smoked away. James Russell Lowell included, in his 1888 book
Heartsease and Rue
, a poem he wrote for a meerschaum pipe given to him as a gift by C. F. Bradford. Oliver Wendell Holmes, in the fifth chapter of his 1858 book
The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table
, compared poetry to meerschaum and the violin, arguing that all three only mature through use.
Fiction, Humor, and Painting
The most concrete example on the prose side is David Christie Murray's story "An Old Meerschaum," which appeared in 1882 in
Coals of Fire and Other Stories
; Bret Harte is also on record as having written a lengthy essay on meerschaum. The humor branch is sharper: Ambrose Bierce, in the 1911 edition of
The Devil's Dictionary

, defined meerschaum as a fine white clay turned into a pipe so it would turn brown, mocking both the material and the mania for coloring it. Mark Twain, according to reports, was the target of a similar joke: in November 1863 in Virginia City, his friends gave him a fake meerschaum pipe as a gift, and Twain, not catching on, delivered a long speech of thanks.

The material found a place in painting as well. American painter Claude Raguet Hirst (1855-1942) is known for her "bachelor still lifes" composed of books, spectacles, matches, and a meerschaum pipe; the pioneer of this vein is considered to be William Harnett, who worked in New York in the same years.
Why Meerschaum?

The first reason for this interest is considered to be the name itself: the word, meaning "sea foam" in German, made the material open to metaphor from the very first mention. The origins of the name and the confusions it caused are covered in detail in the article on the names of meerschaum. The second reason is that carved bowls often carried a figure in their own right. The third is that the coloring process is one that progresses alongside its owner, making it an inherently narratable process. As briar spread in the 20th century, this literature thinned out noticeably.

The name also passed into geography: records show that Meerschaum Canyon and the mining district of the same name in Grant County, New Mexico, take their name from the sepiolite deposits worked there in the early 20th century.

r.x: Briar
(English
briar
, French
bruyère
) is the undisputed king of woods used in pipe making. It is obtained from the underground root burl of the
tree heath
Erica arborea

), which grows across the Mediterranean basin. Tree heath is a shrub that can reach 6-7 meters; but the part that becomes a pipe isn't the trunk, it's this burl that grows between the root and the trunk. Nearly every classic wooden pipe that comes to mind today when someone says "pipe" is made of briar.
Why Briar?
The root burl is a water and nutrient reservoir that lets the plant survive in its arid, fire-prone terrain. This function gives it three properties ideal for a pipe:
Heat resistance:
Its dense, mineral-rich structure withstands the heat of the ember for years.
A balance of lightness and strength:
Despite being hard, it's light enough to be carried in the mouth.
Grain pattern:
The burl's fiber structure forms aesthetic patterns that makers classify under names like "straight grain" and "birdseye."

The hardest and most fire-resistant briar is understood to come from old roots growing slowly on barren, agriculturally unsuitable Mediterranean slopes. Not every burl is usable either: only those that are round and regular in shape are suitable for a pipe, and misshapen ones are already eliminated at harvest.
History
The use of briar in pipe making spread in the mid-19th century, around the French town of
Saint-Claude

. According to the best-known legend, a Frenchman making a pilgrimage to Corsica after Napoleon's death in 1821 had his pipe break along the way, and a local shepherd made him a replacement from briar. It's accepted, however, that the event's actual date falls much later, around the middle of the century; sources do not agree on an exact year.

The claim to origin doesn't belong to Saint-Claude alone: the town of Saint-Paul-de-Fenouillet in the Eastern Pyrenees also argues that the first briar pipe was carved on its own soil. What is documented is this: in October 1858, a shipment of 1,440 rough pipe-blank blocks was delivered from the south to Saint-Claude in a single month — meaning the industry was already established by that date. How the pipe world switched to briar and how Saint-Claude became "the cradle of the pipe" is told in the article on the briar revolution.
From Harvest to Block

Burls are not left to sit after harvest; to prevent them spoiling in transit, sawmills were built close to the harvest areas and, in the early period, ran on water power. At the mill, the burl is cut into two types of block:
Ebauchon:
A rectangular block cut from the interior of the burl; high yield, but random grain direction. It's considered the economic standard of factory production.
Plateaux:
Cut from the bark-covered outer section; larger, and with superior grain orientation. This is why artisan makers prefer plateaux.

Cut blocks are boiled to remove resin and sap; unboiled briar gives a hot smoke with a poor taste either way. Early attempts are said to have "exploded" during smoking when the pipes hadn't been dried; there is also a theory that the boiling technique was inspired by cork-stopper manufacturing in the same region. After boiling, blocks are left to dry naturally in open air for 2-5 years. Rushed drying results in bad taste and cracking when smoked, which is why well-dried briar is considered the first requirement of a quality pipe. The process by which a block becomes a pipe is covered in the article on how a pipe is made, and the finishing techniques applied to the body are covered in surface finishes.
Oil curing
The best-known alternative to natural drying is
oil curing

, patented by Dunhill founder Alfred Dunhill by 1913. In this process, pipes are fitted by their bowls onto brass pins heated by gas flames; over weeks, the hot oil works its way through the fibers, collecting the remaining resin and sap. The method's real purpose wasn't refinement of taste but speed and cost: by drawing off the remaining sap from French briar, it eased the new pipe's break-in period.
The Geography of Briar

The center of gravity of briar sourcing has shifted throughout history: first France and Corsica, then Italy's Calabria, Sicily, and Sardinia regions, Greece, the Algeria-Morocco corridor, and Spain each came to the fore in turn. Today the main sources are known to be Italy, Greece, Spain, and Morocco.
Materials such as meerschaum, corncob, and bog oak are also used as alternatives to briar; for a comparative look, see the article on pipe bowl materials.

r.x: The
history of the clay pipe

begins with tobacco's crossing of the Atlantic and settling into Europe, and traces roughly three centuries in which this cheap, fragile implement remained an everyday object of the common person. The material itself and its manufacturing technique are covered in the clay pipe entry; what's traced here is the arc of the craft's rise and fall.
The Spread of a New Habit

Clay pipe smoking is dated in England to the last quarter of the 16th century, when Virginia tobacco reached the island; the earliest written accounts also belong to this period. Sir Walter Raleigh, known for his New World voyages, is often credited with introducing the habit, though how much of this account rests on documentation versus later legend is debated. What is solidly known through archaeology is that Indigenous peoples of the Americas had used the pipe as a ceremonial implement for centuries.
The new habit met resistance from the start. In 1604, James I published a treatise,
A Counterblaste to Tobacco

, openly attacking tobacco, and that same year raised the import duty to six shillings eightpence per pound. In parts of continental Europe, smokers faced far harsher penalties. On the other hand, tobacco smoke was thought to offer protection during plague outbreaks, and records from the period note that even children were given pipes to smoke under this belief. Neither the tax nor the bans stopped the spread.
Peak and First Decline

Pipe-making found its place within the guild system in the first half of the 17th century and became a distinct trade. Records indicate production peaked around 1680-1700; most town-sized settlements in England had a pipe-maker, and a substantial share of output was exported. In the same century, Dutch cities — Gouda foremost among them — had also become major production centers.

The bowl grew larger in stages over this period. In the early days when tobacco was expensive, bowls were very small; as prices fell and fashion changed, volume increased. Archaeology uses this shift as a dating criterion: a small bowl points to an earlier date. A more measurable indicator is the bore of the stem. According to the sequence J. C. Harrington drew from Virginia finds in 1954, bore diameter runs mostly at 8/64 inch between 1620 and 1650, narrowing to 4/64 inch between 1750 and 1800. Lewis Binford turned this sequence into a regression formula in 1962; later assessments have shown that using the formula alone is unreliable.

Starting in the 1720s, the industry entered a serious contraction. Conflicts across Europe and America hit the export market, and the fashion for snuff among the upper classes pushed the pipe into the background.
A Second Rise and a Quiet End

The clay pipe spread again in the 19th century amid industrial revival and rapid population growth. English, Dutch, French, and German workshops now competed in the same world market, and the way to stand out was through the ornamentation of the mold. Relief motifs can be roughly grouped into three categories: markers of identity and belonging (coats of arms, Masonic symbols, tavern names, advertising slogans), current events (royal ceremonies, sporting matches, well-known faces of the day), and purely decorative figures (plant and animal motifs, mythological scenes). Today, this variety of molds is the primary classification criterion in antique pipe collecting.

th century remained productive in its early years; but by the 1930s demand had fallen off sharply. Cigarettes settling in as a cheap, portable rival, two world wars severing the supply of raw materials and labor, and mass production taking over from everyday handmade objects all played a part together. The clay pipe thus stopped being an everyday item and became a documentary one; today it turns up mostly as a museum piece and excavation find, within historical reenactment communities, and among a limited circle of collectors.

r.x: Professor Stanwell Briar

is a pen name known among pipe enthusiasts. The stories and novels published under this name bring comic fiction and pipe culture together on the same page; in most of the narratives, the lead characters smoke a pipe or a cigar. Records give only the name "Neil" for the author's actual identity; the pen name is used in credits and on book covers. The name itself evokes two familiar words from the pipe world: the Danish manufacturer Stanwell and briar, the primary material of pipe bodies. No explanation from the author regarding this association is known.
From Newspaper to Books

The author's first regular publication was the Agricultural and Mechanical Gazette, a tabloid-format newspaper that came out every other month. Records indicate its first issue appeared in November 1988 and that the publication ended in 1997 with the first issue of volume nine; the newspaper was printed through the author's own resources, without a commercial publisher. The Dirigible Pirates series, serialized in its pages, was later revised and turned into a standalone book called The Dirigible Pirates. This kind of small-scale, reader-direct publishing isn't unusual in pipe and tobacco literature; for similar examples, see the changes in publishing for pipe and tobacco books entry.
The Black Hart Stories

The author's later books gather around a fictional setting called Black Hart. Tales from the Black Hart and The Revenge of Dr. Minneapolis St. Paul are the known links in this series; records indicate other volumes set in the same universe have also been published. A later branch of the series opens into a time-detective narrative under the title Temperance's Temporal Detective Agency; its sequel, Finding Time, has been published on Pipedia in installments.

In these narratives, an invented technology reminiscent of the steam-engine age is intertwined with elements of science fiction; time travel, invented universities, and quietly curious protagonists are recurring elements. The pipe in these texts is not just a set prop; it also functions as a pacing device, marking the moments when a character pauses, thinks, or slows a conversation down.
Place in the Pipe Community

While most who write about pipes and tobacco produce technical or historical texts, this signature chooses to stay within fiction. The community has its own tradition of producing its own writers; names like Regis McCafferty have built the community's memory through magazines and books. Among the better-known examples of the pipe-smoking literary figure is J. B. Priestley. The Professor Stanwell Briar signature sits at the small-scale, humor-leaning end of this tradition. Because information about the person behind the pen name is limited, the author's place in the community is largely traced through the texts and the newspaper; beyond the book credits, no detailed record has been found in independent sources.

r.x: Sanding

is the process by which a pipe body, once out of rough shaping, is worked through progressively finer grits until it reaches its final surface. However unglamorous it may look, this step takes up the largest share of time spent in the workshop. It's not just a polishing prep either: how finely the surface is worked directly determines how much the briar grain will read afterward.
Grit Numbering Systems

Sandpaper grit numbers aren't universal. On the FEPA (ISO 6344) scale common in Europe, the number is preceded by the letter "P"; on the CAMI scale used in North America, that letter is absent. The two systems give fairly close results at coarse grits but diverge noticeably at fine ones. Because of this, sequences described in different sources can't be compared one-to-one; the "600" grit paper one maker names may correspond to quite a different particle size on another scale.
Building the Sequence

The sequences makers follow don't fit a single mold. Reported practices sometimes start at a coarse grit like 120 or 150, sometimes around 220; at the top end, some stop at 800 and say anything finer is imperceptible to the eye, while others carry on to 1000 and even 1500. What's common is that no large jumps are made between consecutive grits, and each paper is worked long enough to fully erase the marks left by the one before.

The first coarse pass is the loudest step in the sequence, but also the most decisive one. A body fresh off the disc or belt sander may look finished but still carries bumps, flats, and machine marks; making the bowl rim perfectly round, cleaning up the line where the shank joins the body, and checking symmetry are also this stage's job. If the shape isn't settled here, cleaning it up at fine grits becomes many times more laborious.
The Rule of Completeness

The unchanging rule of the sequence is that the entire surface, without exception, must be worked at every grit. On shapes with recesses, carving, or sharp transitions this is tiring work, but even a single skipped spot remains visible at later steps. If a missed scratch only shows up during staining, the whole body has to be sanded again at a coarser grit for the color to come out even — meaning a significant portion of the work has to be redone from scratch.

To reduce this risk early on, some makers are reported to wipe a thin guide coat of stain onto the surface midway through the sequence: the stain stays dark inside scratches and gives them away. The method's known drawback is that some of the stain can leave a mark in the wood's pores; as long as that mark won't disrupt the coloring that follows, the technique is a useful control tool.
Sanding the Mouthpiece

The same approach applies to mouthpiece work. Because even the smallest imperfection stands out much faster on smooth-surfaced materials like vulcanite and acrylic than it would on wood, the sequence is usually carried further to finer grits. Once sanding is complete, the pipe is ready for the final surface finishing — staining and felt-wheel buffing.

r.x: The
metal lathe

is a lathe on which the cutting tool isn't held by hand but runs on a slide-mounted carriage. The "metal" in the name signals customary use, not a limit; ebonite, acrylic, and briar are all worked comfortably on the same machine. Within pipe making, the machine's value comes through most clearly on the jobs that most need dimensional precision: the diameter of the mortise, the axis of the bowl, the face of the shank. Setups vary from workshop to workshop; some makers get by with a single lathe, others keep several, each set up for a different job.
How It Differs From a Wood Lathe

On a wood lathe, the maker's own hand holds the tool; the machine offers nothing more than a horizontal tool rest, and shape is entirely up to the hand's judgment. On a metal lathe, the tool is mounted on the carriage and cross slide. This setup constrains the tool's movement, producing cylindrical and tapered surfaces with a repeatability hand work can't match; the top slide, in turn, sets the tool to whatever angle the workpiece requires. A heavier body and tighter manufacturing tolerances round out this precision. When a mouthpiece tenon needs to seat into the shank socket with zero play, the difference is felt directly.
Size and Choosing a Lathe

Lathe size is given by two numbers: the largest workpiece diameter that can swing over the bed, and the distance between headstock spindle and tailstock. A lathe with a 9-inch swing and 20-inch center distance is considered full-size for pipe work; both stummel and mouthpiece are worked on this size. Seven-inch benchtop lathes suffice for mouthpiece work, though a short-bed model can leave a long mouthpiece blank cramped. A known example in this class is Taig, a micro-lathe line made in Arizona, used in workshops mostly for turning mortises and mouthpiece inlay work.

Makers drawn to older machines are far from few. The 9-inch model from South Bend Lathe Works, founded in 1906 in South Bend, Indiana, proved so popular that other manufacturers from England to Brazil turned out near-identical copies; records indicate the firm produced 47 percent of the engine lathes sold annually in the United States in 1930. Old American names like Atlas and Logan also come up frequently in workshop conversations. In England, Myford's ML7, from the company founded in Beeston in 1934, and its improved successor the Super 7 released in 1953, have set the standard in small-scale machine making; for heavier work, Colchester lathes — folded into the 600 Group in 1954 — stand out instead. It's said that a large share of new lathes made in China and sold under importer brand names come off the same factory line, with the difference between them often amounting to little more than the nameplate and included accessories; stripping down and cleaning such a lathe and reassembling it with a good lubrication pass is a common first job.
The Jobs It Handles in the Workshop

A chuck (Jacobs chuck) mounted on the tailstock bores the tobacco chamber, mouthpiece socket, and smoke channel on the axis of rotation; the same setup also faces off the shank. The order and dimensions of these holes are covered in drilling on the lathe. On most lathes the tailstock and headstock spindle sockets are cut to a Morse taper. This taper, developed by Stephen A. Morse in the mid-1860s, self-locks under pressure; standardized across eight sizes from MT0 to MT7, it lets chucks and centers be fitted and removed in a single motion.

Which chuck to use depends on the job. Three-jaw self-centering chucks, with their jaws tied to a shared spiral gear, quickly center a cylindrical mouthpiece blank. In four-jaw independent chucks, each jaw moves separately; this lets a squared-off briar block be gripped and the block offset from center to set the angle for a bent pipe. Some of the chucks made specifically for briar blocks are known as J. T. Cooke-style; in these, the block is turned on locating pins so the bowl axis aligns with the smoke channel.

The lathe's work doesn't stop at drilling. The carriage and cross slide can be used for rough-shaping the stummel. In the shape-first-then-drill method, where the stummel is shaped before drilling, the bit is instead mounted on the headstock spindle and the stummel is brought up to the turning bit by hand. When a tool rest resembling a wood lathe's is fitted onto the slides, hand-held wood-turning tools can also be used. A sanding disc and felt wheel mounted through the spindle bring the shaping and polishing stages onto the same lathe as well. How mouthpiece material behaves on the lathe is covered in mouthpiece materials; part names are covered in pipe anatomy.

r.x: Trever Talbert's approach to design

is often cited as an answer to the question of when drawing should enter the process of handmade pipe making. The American maker founded his own workshop, Talbert Pipes, after winning a national pipe-carving competition organized by a magazine in 1998, and worked for roughly seven years from 2002 onward in the Brittany region of western France. What he says about design describes a working method in which the maker negotiates with the material rather than forcing it into submission from the outset.
A Sketchbook Archive

For Talbert, drawing is an indispensable part of the process. He sketches pipes regularly, working out both how the body will look from the outside and how the smoke channel will run on the inside. But this habit has one distinctive feature: the sketches aren't made for a particular block on the bench — they're produced with no material in front of him at all. Ideas for forms that could suit different grain patterns accumulate over time into a kind of personal vocabulary of shapes.

That vocabulary only becomes functional once he actually picks up the wood. The maker sets aside a handful of drawings that suit the dimensions of the block in front of him and the grain read on its surface, then keeps narrowing the field as the body takes shape. In this way, the confidence of working with tried-and-tested forms is held together with a flexibility that leaves the final word to the block.
Why the Rigid Plan Was Abandoned

Early in his career the maker did the exact opposite: the finished pipe was decided down to the last detail before a single shaving was cut. His reason for abandoning that habit comes straight from the material. Briar comes from a living root; a sand pit, a hairline crack, or an unexpected turn in the grain can turn up in any block. A design fixed to the millimeter on paper has limited room to respond to such a surprise — either the flaw is left in the body or the design is compromised.

Talbert's preference is to cut and rough out the block early and follow the direction the wood points to. This freedom is credited with both reducing waste and creating a more creatively productive working environment.
How the Method Plays Out in the Workshop

The same logic runs through the entire production sequence. After cutting and rough shaping, part of the body is still undecided; drilling and the fine shaping that follows are adjusted to the volume that emerges. The design forms not in a single moment but through a string of small, successive decisions.

The visible result is that no two pipes of the same name are copies of each other. The ability to work flawed areas into the shape also depends on this flexibility. Today the same outlook can be traced in many independent workshops: drawing is treated not as a mandatory specification to be followed, but as a vocabulary the maker draws on while conversing with the material.

r.x: Trever Talbert's finishing method

is the sequence of steps applied at the final stage of a briar pipe, as related by the American maker from his own workshop in the early 2000s. Talbert began making pipes in the 1990s, continued working under the name Talbert Pipes after his success in a 1998 carving competition, and later moved his workshop to France. The description below rests on the maker's account from that period; workshop practices can change over time.
Two Different Paths: Unstained and Stained

The effort spent on finishing depends on the look being aimed for. In Talbert's own distinction, no stain at all is applied to top-grade pieces; the briar is left in its own natural golden-brown tone and simply buffed to a shine.

A stained surface, on the other hand, calls for a far longer process. The maker describes working in repeated layers rather than applying color in a single pass: a dark undercoat is applied, then, once dry, sanded and buffed, followed by another coat. The topcoat color is chosen last, with an eye to how it will read once it filters through the tones beneath it. The goal is not a flat, uniform color but depth in the grain.
The Role of Sanding

In both paths, the bulk of the work lies in sanding. By Talbert's own account, the better the surface is sanded, the better the buffed finish holds, so the workshop runs a wide sandpaper range from 80 to 8000 grit alongside fine steel wool. This range is known only from the maker's own account.
Buffing and Stamping

The final layer is carnauba wax; the lathe, as described, is set up to work with a solid block of carnauba. After buffing, the pipe is stamped: the year it was made, a grade if there is one, any special marks, and the brand logo. The same account notes that at the top grades, called Signature and Minaria, a hand-carved signature was used instead of the logo stamp. These names no longer appear on the brand's current grading page.

Indeed, the system has since changed. According to official information, the tiered grading of the Talbert Briar line was dropped in 2020, and pipes began carrying a single brand stamp instead. The entry-level Ligne Bretagne line uses a numbering system running from 1 to 5, moving from a fully rustic surface to a flawlessly smooth one. Year-stamping, however, has continued.

Once the pipe receives its final hand buffing, it is considered finished from the workshop's standpoint. Reading this entry alongside the same maker's accounts of drilling and fine shaping makes it easier to see how a pipe moves from start to finish in a one-person workshop.

r.x: The
briar used in Dr. Grabow pipes

is one of the rare subjects that allows a step-by-step look at exactly how a mass-production factory sorts its raw material. The company, making pipes in Sparta, North Carolina since 1943, still produces, by its own account, roughly two hundred thousand pipes a year from Mediterranean briar. The brand's model names aren't randomly chosen labels: which line a block enters is decided by two gradings it passes through after arriving at the factory. The practice described below belongs mostly to the period between the 1960s and the late 1980s and rests largely on the account of a source who worked at the factory.
Seven Grades by Flaw Count

Blocks that arrive by the sackful are roughly turned and sanded before going through dry grading. At this stage, grain isn't considered at all; only the number of flaws in the wood is the basis, and blocks are ranked from one to seven. Grade one is flawless, grade two's few small voids are easily filled, and grade three becomes a smooth-finish pipe with the help of filler. Grades four through six can only carry a rustic finish; grade seven is, in practice, scrap. This ranking explains why surface finishes in factory pipes are considered a matter of grading as much as of style.
Grain Letter and Model Line

Blocks in the first two grades also go through a wet grading: an alcohol-water mixture applied to the surface (reportedly a fifty-fifty methanol and water mix) makes the grain visible, and the result is lettered from A to H. A and E show full grain, B and F show roughly three-quarters, C and G show half; D and H fall below that. According to the same account, the letter directly corresponded to a model line: full-grain blocks went to top lines such as Emperor, Eldorado, Sculptura, and Starfire; three-quarter-grain to Regal and Silver Duke; half-grain to Willard's smooth-finish examples; and weak-grain blocks to stained models such as Color Duke and Color Viscount; Westbrook, distributed through R. J. Reynolds coupons, was also fed by full-grain blocks. Since this mapping rests on a single factory source, it shouldn't be taken as a definitive chart. The lines the brand carries today are named Duke, Lark, Grand Duke, Royal Duke, Riviera, and Savoy.
What's in the Sack

Mills sell briar in five selections: plateaux, Extra Extra, Extra, First, and Mixed. Plateaux blocks are cut adjacent to the burl's bark and so give regular grain, and are used mostly in freehand pipes; Dr. Grabow has almost never turned to this selection. The remaining four selections are distinguished by the proportion of top-grade blocks each yields: reportedly, roughly three-quarters of an Extra Extra sack falls into the first two grades, a ratio that drops to half in Extra, a third in First, and a tenth in Mixed.

Flawed blocks aren't simply discarded either. Those cut in Europe with a shortened shank allowance were used with a band; "chip top" blocks that fell short in height were lowered from the top; and pieces with one or a few narrow faces went to the factory's flat-panel-cutting machinery. Most of the squared-off Duke examples with no counterpart on the shape chart are said to originate here, and the small offcuts that never get graded at all are reported to be routed into the Duke and Lark lines. This is where the difference between factory pipes and artisan pipes becomes clear: in mass production, the real skill lies in finding a suitable place for every block that comes out of the same sack.
From Burl to Sack

Briar is the underground root burl of the Mediterranean tree heath (Erica arborea). The burl is kept wet until cut; at the mill it's first split in two, then divided into rectangular blocks called ebauchon. Blocks are boiled in large vats to be purged of tannin and sap, then air-dried and sacked. The direction of the cut is named along with the block: "M" is cut for straight pipes, "R" for bent and Continental shapes. The factory's briar is stated to come mostly from Greece, with the rest from Italy and Spain.

r.x: Briar block sourcing

is the first decision a pipe maker makes before ever sitting down at the bench. The briar burl is dug from the ground, cut into blocks at the sawmill, boiled, and left to dry for a long stretch of time; by the time it reaches the maker's hands, it carries a chain of processing stretched over years. Which link of that chain a block was taken from determines how much the maker can actually know about the wood in hand. Briar sourcing is therefore not treated as a matter of shopping in pipe making, but as an extension of material knowledge.
Two Block Forms Set by the Cut

Whoever cuts the burl into blocks chooses, with every cut, between two goals: maximizing the number of pieces obtained, or favoring the grain direction of the pieces. This choice is why two distinct forms of wood reach workshops.
A cut favoring piece count yields
ebauchon

. Taken from the interior of the burl, these blocks are roughly rectangular and square-edged; their surfaces are trued at the sawmill, so they are easy to fix on the lathe. Where the grain will fall, however, is left largely to chance. The great majority of briar pipes are understood to come from this type of block.
A cut favoring grain direction yields
plateaux

. Taken from the outer part of the burl, these pieces resemble a quarter circle, are larger than ebauchon, and carry on their outer face the hard bark that was in contact with the soil. Few plateaux come out of any given burl. Pipes with pronounced straight grain are almost always made from plateaux blocks. The relationship between block form and the pattern that surfaces is covered separately in the article on grain.
How Knowable Is the Wood's History
Blocks reach workshops through three structural channels. These channels form a hierarchy in terms of how traceable the wood's history is.

The end with the highest traceability is working directly with a sawmill. Which batch the wood came from, how long it was held, and how it was stored are all known; moreover, material arrives in large volumes of consistent quality. Against this, almost every sawmill sets a minimum order quantity, which means far more blocks than an occasional pipe maker could use up in years. Because nearly all the burls that feed the pipe trade come from the Mediterranean basin, a buyer outside the region also has to reckon with import and international payment logistics.

In the middle stand established makers with long-standing relationships with sawmills. Wood sold by a maker who supplies enthusiasts and young makers from his own stock is of known quality, since it comes from the same batch he uses himself; ready-made sets pre-drilled to a requested size may also be available. This route carries a benefit independent of the wood itself: the buyer also gains access to someone knowledgeable to consult.

The end with the lowest traceability is firms dealing in pipe-making materials and tools. This is the most practical channel for small quantities, and the wood that arrives is often of good quality; but how many years the block was held and under what conditions it was stored generally goes unrecorded. Because these firms operate on wholesale terms, the sawmill the wood comes from can vary from order to order. The same channel also carries pre-drilled blocks with the mortise already fitted; here the geometry of the airway is already resolved, leaving only shape work.
A Block Unknown Until Cut

What is inside a block cannot be known until it is cut; the bark and dimensions visible from outside give no warning of an internal crack or sand pit. The maker's only real anchor is therefore the wood's history: which sawmill it came from, how long it was dried, and how it was stored. A block whose curing was left incomplete behaves unpredictably on the lathe, and wood that hasn't dried enough keeps working even after it's been shaped. This is why sources written on pipe making treat sourcing as a separate heading in its own right.

r.x: The
global spread of briar pipe makers

describes how, since the mid-20th century, the number of countries where briar pipes are made entirely by a single person has multiplied many times over. This trade was once confined to a handful of centers in France, England, Italy, and Denmark; today, workshops of a few people operate on most continents. The boundaries of the term "artisan," used for this segment of the community, remain a matter of debate.
Origins of the Term and the Movement

The habit of distinguishing a pipe hand-shaped by its own maker from factory production is understood to have taken root in Denmark after the Second World War. The pioneer of this distinction is generally cited as Sixten Ivarsson (1910-2001), Swedish-born but working in Copenhagen; some accounts date the beginning of the movement directly to his work in the 1960s. His search for shapes beyond classic English molds is associated with his name and set the standard for the generation of Danish makers that followed. Reportedly, among those he trained were Jess Chonowitsch, his son Lars Ivarsson, and the Japanese maker Kazuhiro Fukuda. This sensibility, which took shape around Ivarsson, is known today as the Danish School.

In Italy, a similar break occurred in the same years: Carlo Scotti launched the Castello brand with the workshop he founded in Cantù, in the province of Como, in 1947, and reworked classic shapes in his own idiom. The word itself, however, took on this meaning much later: major pipe books from the 1980s through the early 2000s don't use "artisan" in its present-day sense. The term's current usage dates to roughly the same period as the spread of the internet, the last fifteen to twenty years. For a detailed distinction, see the article on artisan pipes and factory pipes.
A Sixty-Two-Country Tally

No official body tracks the size of this community; the figures available come from records kept by individual researchers. The most extensive one published is a personal compilation that appeared on Pipedia in September 2025, putting the number of countries with briar pipe makers at 62. The same compiler's 2022 article put the figure at 54. The most heavily represented rows in the record are the US (442), Italy (207), Denmark (139), Germany (137), and Great Britain (100); followed by France (59), Russia (43), Sweden (33), and China (29). Canada and Japan each carry 24 names, Spain 22, Czechia 21, and Ukraine 20. Countries such as Albania, Algeria, New Zealand, Vietnam, and South Korea are represented by a single name; Türkiye appears with two entries.

The compilation has no independent verification, and its compiler is explicit about its limits: the list doesn't separate factory brands from one-person workshops into different rows, keeps deceased makers on the list, and counts entities such as Scotland, Hong Kong, and Crimea as separate rows. The figure should therefore be read less as the trade's actual population than as a map of the records one researcher was able to access. Three-quarters of the 1,481 names in the table are still concentrated in the US, Italy, Denmark, Germany, Great Britain, and France; the real shift is not that production has moved away from these centers but that the number of countries on the list has grown. Forty-four countries show fewer than ten names, and twenty of these show only a single maker.
An Institutional Gap

No professional body represents a community this scattered, either. The association founded in 1933 as the Retail Tobacco Dealers of America is on record as having become the International Premium Cigar & Pipe Retailers Association in 2007 and the Premium Cigar Association in 2019; with each name change it narrowed its scope around cigar retailing and today has no ties to pipe makers. The quarterly magazine
Pipes and tobaccos

, which had regularly featured makers, also closed in 2019 after its publisher changed hands. What remains of this communication now runs largely through forums, annual pipe gatherings, and social media. The broader framework of how production methods have changed is covered in the article on pipe making.

r.x: Meerschaum
is the pipe world's strongest tie to Türkiye. Scientifically named
sepiolite
, this mineral has for centuries been one of pipe making's most prized materials for its light, soft, porous structure. Its German-derived international name,
Meerschaum

, means "sea foam" — a nod to the stone's whiteness and lightness. The comparison isn't unfounded either: with a density close to water's, and able to dip below it in dry blocks, meerschaum is one of the very few minerals that can float on water. The name "sepiolite" was coined in the 19th century by German mineralogist E. F. Glocker; derived from the Greek
sepia
, the name points to the stone's resemblance to cuttlebone.
Eskişehir's White Gold
The mineral sepiolite is found in many places around the world, from Greece to Spain, Morocco to the United States; but the commercially worked deposits of
block meerschaum
suitable for pipe making are, in practice, found only around
Eskişehir

. This exclusivity has also earned the stone names such as "Eskişehir stone," "white gold," and "aktaş" (white stone). The mines are clustered in a narrow area near the city; the stone is still extracted largely by traditional shaft-and-gallery methods and simple tools, from shafts running tens of meters down to depths exceeding 300 meters. At around 2 on the Mohs scale, the stone is soap-soft when it comes out of the mine still damp; carvers work extraordinarily detailed pipes — from sultans' busts to dragon figures — while the stone is still in this fresh state. As it dries it grows lighter and harder, becoming a powerful absorber of liquids and gases. Passed down through generations, Eskişehir meerschaum carving is today counted among Türkiye's living cultural heritage practices.
Two types are distinguished in the market:
block meerschaum
, meaning a solid natural nodule, and
pressed meerschaum

, made by pressing shavings and fragments with a binder. Large, crack-free, white, and homogeneous blocks are the most valuable; pressed stone, having largely lost its porosity and carvability, is considered second-tier.
From Vienna Stone to Local Mastery

Meerschaum was one of the Ottoman Empire's important export items from the 18th century onward. For roughly three centuries the raw stone was shipped to Europe, chiefly Vienna, and carved there into pipes and figurines; this is why the stone was long known in Europe as "Vienna stone." Thousands of workers are recorded as employed in Eskişehir's mines in the 1800s. Once raw-stone exports were gradually restricted and then fully banned in the second half of the 20th century, carving took root in Eskişehir itself, and Türkiye gained a de facto world monopoly on block meerschaum. The pioneer of domestic carving is credited to Eskişehir craftsman
Ali Osman Denizköpüğü
, who took his surname from the stone's name. For the Ottoman pipe tradition's İstanbul-based craft branch, see Tophane lüle craft.

The stone's fame has even lent its name and form to pipes made of other materials: the American firm that mass-produced the corn cob pipe named itself Missouri Meerschaum in homage to the stone; the combustion chamber that seats into the gourd body of the calabash pipe is also traditionally made from meerschaum.
Smoking Character
What sets meerschaum apart from briar comes down to these features:
Cool, dry smoke:
the porous structure absorbs moisture, nicotine, and tar, letting the tobacco's flavor come through as it is.
Neutral taste:
unlike briar it adds no character of its own and holds no ghost aroma, so very different blends can be smoked one after another in the same bowl.
No resting or breaking-in required:
unlike briar pipes, performance loss over back-to-back smokes is far smaller, and no break-in period is needed.
The maintenance difference: no cake wanted

A classic mistake carried over from briar habits is letting a cake layer build up in meerschaum. The layer that protects the bowl in briar is harmful in meerschaum: it clogs the pores and, expanding at a different rate than the stone, can crack the bowl — which is why the bowl is regularly wiped and kept cake-free. Because of its fragility, meerschaum pipes also call for careful handling; most are sold with their own hard case.
Patina: The Stone's Living Color
Meerschaum's most captivating trait is that it
changes color

as it's smoked. Absorbed tobacco compounds coat the stone in a patina that moves from the bottom of the bowl toward the rim — first honey, then amber, deepening over years to a dark reddish brown; wax applied to the pipe's surface both speeds up and deepens this coloring. An old meerschaum pipe with an even, well-developed patina carries both aesthetic and material value for collectors.

r.x: African blackwood
, known in East Africa by its Swahili name
mpingo
and botanically as
Dalbergia melanoxylon

, is a small savanna tree of the legume family. It is sometimes also known in trade as "grenadilla." Its timber is counted among the densest and hardest wood materials known; in pipe making this density is both an advantage and a source of difficulty.
The Tree and Its Wood

Mpingo grows in seasonally arid regions in a belt stretching from Senegal to Eritrea, south through Tanzania and Mozambique to the northeast of South Africa. Its height generally stays between 4 and 15 meters, and its trunk is often forked and irregular; this makes obtaining large, flawless blocks difficult. The tree takes more than sixty years to mature.

The heartwood is almost entirely black, in some pieces leaning toward dark brown or purple, with a grain pattern hard to make out with the naked eye. The surrounding sapwood, by contrast, is very thin and pale yellow; the sharp color contrast between the two layers is the material's most recognizable feature. Its measured average density runs around 1,270 kg/m³, meaning it sinks in water. Measurement tables give its Janka hardness as 3,670 lbf; this value places it at the very top rank among trees traded commercially.
Use in Pipe Making

Mpingo is not a bowl wood like briar; its place in pipe making is mostly as a complementary component. Thanks to its high density, which lends itself to fine threading and holding sharp detail, it is known to be favored for shank extensions, tenon bands, and decorative rings. Some makers are also said to cut the mouthpiece (stem) body itself from this wood; for its place among mouthpiece materials, see the mouthpiece materials entry.

Working the material is not easy. Because it quickly dulls cutting edges, it is difficult to shape with either hand tools or machinery; this is why it is often shaped on metalworking lathes in instrument workshops. On the lathe, however, it gives an exceptionally clean surface and reaches a deep gloss even without finishing. For general use of woods other than briar in pipes, comparisons are offered in the woods other than briar in pipes and alternative woods used in pipe making entries.
Conservation Concern

Mpingo is also the primary body wood for wind instruments such as the clarinet, oboe, and bagpipe; this demand has placed heavy pressure on the slow-growing species. The species is assessed as "near threatened" on the IUCN Red List. Because the entire
Dalbergia

genus falls under CITES Appendix II, international trade, including in processed products, is subject to documentation requirements. Among the initiatives built on sustainable harvesting and replanting, the leading ones are the Mpingo Conservation & Development Initiative and the African Blackwood Conservation Project, both working in Tanzania. For this reason, the mpingo used in pipe workshops mostly comes from small offcuts left over from the instrument-making industry.

r.x: Briar calabash shapes

cover a broad family that recreates, in a single piece of wood, the silhouette of the two-piece gourd pipe. The two ends of the family don't much resemble one another: in one, the bowl sits as a separate mass above the body; in the other, the bowl mouth is cut flush with the body. What actually qualifies a pipe as a calabash is, for this reason, a subject collectors return to regularly.
The Criterion: Where the Bowl Sits on the Gourd Pipe

The basis of the distinction is the structure of the calabash pipe itself. The 1909 Circular No. 41 that David Fairchild and G. N. Collins prepared for the US Department of Agriculture describes step by step the cultivation of the South African pipe gourd (Lagenaria): while the neck is still soft it is bent to the desired angle with stakes fixed into perforated boards, once dried and hardened the wide end is cut off, the bowl is set in place with plaster mortar, and the exposed surface of the mortar is wrapped in a thin strip of cork. The pipe plate in the same publication shows the meerschaum bowl seated on the body at one of two possible heights. If the bowl is set into the neck, leaving the gourd's outer profile untouched, it counts as a sunken cup; if it caps the gourd like a hood and overhangs the edges, it counts as a top bowl. Early gourd pipes are also known in which the sunken cup was covered with a silver lid.
Sunken Cup and Bell Bodies

In briar, the sunken-cup interpretation is achieved by applying a flat cut to the mouth of a body that imitates the gourd's curve; the bowl doesn't read as a separate piece from outside. Castello's shape 49 is the most frequently cited example of this group. Some Brebbia models fall into the same line; a few curved calabashes from Barling, a maker mostly known for straight pipes, are also counted here.

A subgroup of the family is the "bell" shape, where the body flares outward toward the bowl mouth: the top line is still cut flat, but the sides widen upward. Peterson's XL05 shape is the most often cited representative of this form; Dunhill, Ferndown, and Sasieni have also produced bell interpretations. Degree of curve falls outside the criterion: although calabash brings to mind a deeply curved silhouette, straight or slightly curved examples belong to the same family. Stanwell's well-known calabash shape is recorded as a design by Jess Chonowitsch and is only lightly curved.
Top Bowl Interpretations
On the top-bowl side, pipes are distinguished not by shape but by the route taken to reach that shape. Three basic solutions are known.
Carved from a single block.

The impression of an overhanging bowl is cut from the same briar piece as the body. The calabashes in Ser Jacopo's Picta series are the best-known example of this route; Ardor, Rinaldo, and Butz-Choquin work in a similar way.
Glued-on cap.

A separate cap is fixed to the body. Teddy Knudsen's boxwood-capped calabashes are the best-known example of this technique; the cap may also be briar, olivewood, or acrylic. Cavicchi and Il Ceppo follow a similar path.
Detachable bowl.
The bowl sits as an independent piece atop the body, echoing the two-piece construction of the gourd pipe in a different material. Some Ascorti models belong to this group.
Where the Term Stands

The distinction doesn't promise sharp boundaries. Some models, such as Ashton's LX Sovereign, carry features of both groups at once: the body widens upward while the top of the bowl is finished domed rather than flat. The top bowl / sunken cup / bell / straight distinction was put forward as a discussion proposal by Fred Heim in The Pipe Collector, the bulletin of the American pipe collectors' association NASPC. Since there's no central classification authority for pipe shapes, these terms are not treated as an industry standard; even so, they are credited with making it easier to describe the differences within the calabash family on a historical basis.

r.x: The
frazing machine
is the name used in pipe workshops for the copy-milling machine that mechanically transfers a shape held ready on a metal master pattern onto a briar block. The term's kinship with the French verb
fraiser

, meaning to mill, is often mentioned; but this connection is more a linguistic association than something documented in the pipe literature. In Turkish it's rendered as "copy mill" or "pattern-following machine."
Working Principle

A metal sample representing all or part of the shape to be produced is fixed to one side of the machine. On the other side, an unbored raw body (stummel) is secured. As a follower tip travels along the surface of the pattern, a cutter mechanically linked to it travels the same path over the briar and removes excess material. The motion is transmitted from one end to the other through arms, joints, and counterweights; numerical control or computer data play no part. Similar mechanisms have long been used in fields like furniture making, foundry mold work, and gunstock making; what sets the pipe machine apart is that it works with a relatively small piece of material, each specimen of which has a different density.
Its Place in Factory Production

Because it's the practical way to produce many copies of the same shape, copy milling is considered the backbone of factory workshops. When a catalogue shape needs to be reproduced repeatedly to standard dimensions, the machine comes into play; this has let production in centers like Saint-Claude sustain dozens of models consistently. The result the machine produces, however, is not a finished pipe. The body coming off the machine carries cutter marks, sharp transitions, and excess wood; these need to be cleaned by file, sandpaper, and hand. This is why a considerable portion of even factory pipes is completed by hand. The method suits the classic pipe shapes family in particular: forms with defined proportions, like billiard, apple, or bulldog, can be reproduced from a pattern without deviation. That the same machine can be switched to a different model by swapping the pattern has also made it easier for workshops to sustain a broad shape repertoire with limited equipment.
Relationship to Handmade Work

Some makers never turn to the copy machine at all. The argument given is that developing a shape through the partnership of eye and hand gives a more settled result; since every block's grain and flaws differ, the only way to adapt the shape to the wood is to work it by hand. The freehand approach is born largely out of this stance. Even in most workshops that do use the machine, it handles only the rough-shaping stage, not the whole of the design; what follows is still determined by the maker.

Community accounts say that few original examples of the old machines survive today; the equipment of closed factories has mostly been discarded or refurbished. Because this information rests largely on oral tradition, it isn't possible to give a numerical tally.

r.x: Drilling vulcanite rod

is the first and most decisive step in making a pipe mouthpiece. Although the mouthpiece looks, from the outside, like nothing more than a shape, its real function is carried out by the smoke channel inside it; once that channel is drilled crooked, rough, or off-center, correcting it afterward is next to impossible. That's why craftsmen open the hole before they ever shape the rod.
Nature of the Material

Vulcanite is a hard mass obtained by vulcanizing natural rubber with a high proportion of sulfur over a long period; it's also known as ebonite. The sulfur ratio varies over a wide range depending on the formulation, and the region that gives the best mechanical strength is generally taken to be around one third. Industrial-scale use of the material became established after Charles Goodyear developed vulcanization, when his brother Nelson Goodyear obtained a patent for hard rubber in 1851. Vulcanite cuts cleanly on the lathe and polishes well by hand; on the other hand, it's sensitive to heat. Worked at high speed or with a clogged bit, the surface burns, gives off an odor, and discolors. Its comparison with other materials used for mouthpieces is covered in the mouthpiece materials entry.
The Logic of Drilling

The operation is carried out on a metal lathe, where it isn't the bit that turns but the material. The advantage of this reversed arrangement is centering: when a rod chucked in a self-centering chuck spins and the bit is only pressed lightly against it, the material draws the bit toward the middle of its own axis. That's why the face of the rod is trued up first; a crooked face throws the bit off to one side on the very first contact. Once the starting hole is opened, the tailstock is locked and feed continues under controlled pressure.

The channel isn't opened at a single diameter but in stages. The end of the mouthpiece that sits against the pipe is widened into a funnel shape with a tapered bit — reportedly around 9/64 inch — and since this widening needs to stop roughly a centimeter short of the rod's other end, a mark is made on the bit's shaft beforehand. The remaining long section is finished with a fine 1/16-inch bit. The channel thus ends up with a cross-section that starts wide on the pipe side and narrows toward the bit end. The general principles of drilling are gathered in the drilling on the lathe entry.
Heat, Chips and Surface

The main risk in this operation is heat. Because thin, long drill bits have shallow flutes for clearing chips, debris builds up inside the hole; the accumulated chips increase friction and the vulcanite quickly burns, leaving an odor and dulling in color. To prevent this, the lathe is kept at the lowest speed, the bit is withdrawn and cleaned frequently, and feed is achieved with patience rather than pressure.

Once the hole is opened, the inner surface remains rough. A common fix is to wrap a strip of fine sandpaper around the bit's shaft and smooth the inside of the channel, again at low speed, working through progressively finer grits. The final section widened with the tapered bit can't be worked at this stage; the wrapped bit doesn't reach that far in. This isn't considered a shortcoming, because that part will be reopened anyway when the mouthpiece is fitted to the pipe. The drilled rod then moves on to tenon turning and exterior shaping — in other words, to mouthpiece work.

r.x: The
fake meerschaum pipe attributed to Gustav Fischer

is considered the longest-running and most widely circulated forgery case in antique pipe collecting. Featuring dancing couples on the bowl, a dark reddish-brown color, and a metal band on the shank, this piece has kept resurfacing since the mid-1990s. It's not a single specimen but a run of many copies from the same mold; though it's often described in listings as meerschaum, the pipe is neither meerschaum nor any of the known imitation-stone compositions of its supposed period.
The Start of the Suspicion

Records show the piece was first submitted for expert opinion in October 1994: a London auction house sent a photograph of the pipe in its possession, asking for information about its maker. The correspondence stated that the pipe was carved from amber, and that it bore the signature "Gustav Fisher Jnr" on the bowl and "Gustav Fisher, Vienna, Exposition 1873" on the mouthpiece. The piece was not put up for sale following the review. The place the piece was first exhibited with photographs in print was Ben Rapaport's 1999 book from Schiffer Publishing,
Collecting Antique Meerschaum Pipes: Miniature to Majestic Sculpture
Contradictions in the Signature

The detail that actually exposes the forgery is the signature itself. To start, the surname is misspelled: the carver who worked in Boston was named Gustav Fischer, not "Fisher"; a maker misspelling his own name is not to be expected. The language of the inscription is also inconsistent. An Austrian-born carver referring to the exhibition in question would have written, in German, "Wien Ausstellung 1873"; the English wording strengthens the impression that the signature was fabricated after the fact. The exhibition itself is real — the Weltausstellung 1873 Wien, which opened on May 1, 1873 — but that doesn't validate the signature.

The "Jnr" suffix throws the chronology off entirely: the son bearing the same name was born in 1887 in Manhattan and worked only with briar, so it's impossible for his name to appear on a pipe referencing an 1873 exhibition. Finally, records indicate that Gustav Fischer Sr. mostly left his pipes unsigned. The name of this maker, who lived from 1847 to 1937, has over the years also been attached to other antique meerschaums he never touched, with catalogue descriptions crediting him with work that wasn't his.
Material and Craftsmanship

Most of the tells distinguishable even from a photograph are in the material. The bowl is not carved but cast in a mold; the mold seam running along its underside is visible to the naked eye. The color isn't a patina earned through smoking either: the piece is given a deep oxblood tone from day one, whereas a bowl coming from the master's hand emerges milk-white and gains its color over time. The carving is crude, with weak detail. The mouthpiece is plain plastic, not amberoid pressed from amber or amber fragments; this distinction is detailed in the article on mouthpiece materials. The shank band, meanwhile, is a cast zinc alloy rather than silver or gold. It's been assessed that the body could be epoxy, cast resin, or high-strength plaster; the place of these materials in pipe making is covered in the article on hydrostone and resin pipes.
Circulation and the Lesson

Since the mid-2000s, the same pipe has appeared repeatedly at auctions in England, France, and America, on online marketplaces, and on image-sharing sites. Some catalogues openly list the piece as a "reproduction," while others have listed it as a genuine late-19th-century antique meerschaum; there are also listings that don't mention the material at all. Its manufacturer has never been identified. The real lesson this case leaves for collecting is that a signature alone cannot count as documentation: verification starts with the material, the craftsmanship, and historical consistency. For a comparable case on the briar side, see the article on the fake Dunhills of the 1980s.

r.x: Turning tenons

is the process of turning down the cylindrical projection at the end of the mouthpiece (stem) to the diameter that will fit the mortise bored into the shank. This is the single surface that joins the pipe's two parts together, which is why it's considered the least forgiving stage of pipe making. Even a deviation of one percent of an inch in tenon diameter changes whether the fit ends up loose or forced. For its place in the overall process, see the how a pipe is made entry.
Tolerance and Equipment

This is not a scale that can be held to with a wood lathe's dial; the work is mostly done on a metal lathe. What the metal lathe brings isn't so much precision as repeatability: a second part machined at the same setting matches the dimension of the first. The Taig Micro Lathe II, common in small workshops, is described in manufacturer and distributor documentation as capable of roughly 0.0005-inch working precision. Since the same lathe is also used in the workshop for drilling on the lathe, the mortise and tenon are often prepared on a single machine and with a single sense of axis.
The Mortise Sets the Size

Although there's a rough target diameter kept in mind for the tenon, the final size isn't set on paper — it's set in that particular pipe's own mortise; every briar block reacts slightly differently to drilling. The test is done without removing the mouthpiece from the lathe. Once a part is taken out of the chuck it never sits back in its old axis exactly; getting a round surface on the new axis requires taking off a considerable amount of material, and if the target diameter has already been approached, that allowance no longer exists. The result is an off-axis tenon.

The fit is meant to be tight at the first assembly, because it's known that the joint loosens somewhat as the pipe is used; the reason for that loosening hasn't been fully clarified in the community either. On the other hand, there's a limit to how much force thin shanks can take: pressing an overly tight tenon into the mortise can crack the shank. Nor is it mandatory for the tenon to be cut from the mouthpiece itself; see the entries on using a separate Delrin tenon, and on the spacers used at the shank-mouthpiece joint, mouthpiece spacers.
Cutting Tool, Speed and Surface

A clean surface largely depends on the sharpness of the cutting tool: a dull tool tears the material as it cuts, leaving a mark that then has to be removed with sandpaper. Makers working with a high-speed steel (HSS) tool are reported to resharpen it for every mouthpiece. As for speed, turning behaves the opposite of drilling; a higher speed gives a smoother surface.

Diameter is monitored with calipers as the work proceeds. Common practice is to stop a few thousandths of an inch above the target diameter, leaving the remaining allowance to fine sandpaper and then to a light wax polish. It's also noted that if the cutting tool is sharp enough, that leftover allowance can be reduced.
