r.x: Making
pipes from woods other than briar

is a branch of pipe smoking born partly of necessity and partly of curiosity. The benchmark material, briar, comes from the burl that forms on the root of tree heath (Erica arborea); the fact that this wood is extremely hard, dense, and heat-resistant sets it apart among bowl woods. Even so, a usable bowl can be obtained from most hardwoods. Cherry, olive, maple, walnut, and oak are, after briar and bog oak, the species most often mentioned among pipe bowl materials.
The Forced Substitute of the War Years

In the United States during World War II, briar burls that could no longer be imported were replaced by the root burls of mountain laurel (Kalmia latifolia). This choice was no accident: mountain laurel and the tree heath that yields briar both belong to the heath family (Ericaceae), and both form a hard, tangle-grained burl at the root crown. The same years are said to have seen North European workshops turn to beech. Wooden pipe smoking before briar already rested on a similar logic; Ulm burl-wood pipes were carved from burls of alder, walnut, pear, and maple.
How the Species Behave

r.x: The most concrete advantage of non-briar species is weight. Because most of these woods are lower in density than briar, even a thick-walled, large-bowled pipe can stay light in the hand and mouth. But lightness usually comes bundled with softness: in soft wood the drill and countersink don't cut cleanly, and the bowl wall can char before the carbon layer settles. At the other end of the scale, very dense species see the opposite problem; drying and heat cracks are commonly reported in woods like ebony and hawthorn.
Unsuitable Species and Points of Caution

Softwoods like pine, spruce, and cedar are resinous and soft and are not considered bowl material; they tend to burn before a carbon layer can form. The wood used must also be fully dried; a green or half-dry block inevitably cracks once worked. Correctly identifying the species is a separate matter in its own right: the sap and dust of some trees carry irritant compounds, and mountain laurel, the war years' favored substitute, is considered toxic in every part of the plant. This is why makers place great importance on positively identifying an unfamiliar wood before using it in a bowl.
Finishing and Longevity

Leaving non-briar woods unstained and finishing only with sanding and polish is a common practice among makers; the fine grain detail and pale colors of these species tend to be muted rather than emphasized under stain. The remaining finishing steps are the same as for briar. As for durability, most problems tend to surface within the first few smokes; a bowl that gets through break-in without cracking is reported to hold up well thereafter.

r.x: The
drill press

is a stationary drilling machine that, thanks to its column-mounted body and vertical spindle, holds the bit on the same axis with every plunge. Its role in the pipe workshop can be summed up in one sentence: the bowl, smoke channel, and mortise bored into a briar block have to align to within a fraction of a millimeter, and a hand-held drill can't hold that alignment. The machine's value in the workshop comes not from its power but from the angle between spindle and table never changing — that is, from holes drilled at the same setting repeating each other exactly.
Setup and Clamping the Block

Drilling doesn't start until the block is secured to the table. The usual way is a machine vise; it both grips the block firmly and slides finely across the table so the bit lands exactly where intended. For angled bowls or curved channels, the axis is changed by tilting the vise or the table; the bit still comes down vertically while the block meets it at the desired angle.

At what stage the block gets drilled is a matter of workshop preference. Some makers mount the raw block directly on the machine and drill first, shaping the form afterward around those axes; others rough out the shape first, then drill. This distinction is treated separately under shape first, then drill, and in the community it's seen not as a hard rule but as a difference in habit.
The Machine's Limits

How well a given machine suits pipe work is largely judged by three settings. The first is speed: low speed is considered essential for a clean, unburned hole in briar that doesn't drift off axis. On cheap models, speed is changed in steps by moving a belt between pulleys by hand; higher-end machines have a variable-speed motor. The second is the table's ability to raise and lower — an adjustment found on nearly every machine that can seem trivial, but which factors directly into pipe work by letting the block move closer to the spindle and make full use of the available plunge.

The real constraint lies in the third: the distance the quill can travel in a single plunge, the stroke. This distance is the upper limit on how long a hole can be drilled, and on ordinary machines it's measured in a few centimeters. That's no problem for a short-shanked billiard; it's pushed to the limit on long-shanked shapes like the Canadian or hawkbill. That's why most makers turn to drilling on the lathe for long smoke channels, where depth is set not by the quill but by the length of the bit and the lathe bed.
Its Relationship to the Lathe

The drill press isn't the only drilling tool in the workshop. Because the metal lathe allows both deeper holes and finishing the mortise and shank work in a single setup, a significant share of experienced makers gravitate to the lathe over time. Even so, the press doesn't disappear from the workshop entirely: because it's quick to set up and easy to learn, it stays in use for the bowl's initial hole, mouthpiece bores, and various auxiliary jobs. Shaping and sanding, meanwhile, are the domain of entirely different machines like the belt sander.

r.x: Pipe filters and systems

is the collective name for solutions aimed at reducing the amount of moisture and tar that reaches the mouth during a smoke. Three main approaches have developed: absorbent filters fitted into the slot between shank and stem (activated carbon, balsa, paper), metal condensing devices that gather the moisture in the smoke (the stinger), and "system" pipes that carry a reservoir for moisture within the body itself. All share the same goal — a drier, cooler smoke, which in turn reduces the risk of tongue bite. Filter use is largely a regional tradition: the 9 mm filter is the de facto standard in Germany and Central Europe, while unfiltered smoking dominates the English-American world.
Absorbent Filters: Activated Carbon and Balsa

The history of the modern pipe filter begins with the German firm Vauen. The "Dr. Perl" brand, based on the smoke-filtering work of Berlin chemist Jacques Perl, was registered in 1921; the first product was a paper filter in 6 and 9 mm lengths. The Dr. Perl junior, launched in 1934, was the world's first activated-carbon pipe filter, and Vauen held the patent for this invention for about twenty years. The innovation gradually led most German and Austrian pipes to be drilled with a 9 mm filter chamber. Savinelli, taking a different path, uses rods cut from porous balsa wood; balsa works by absorbing moisture and is considered neutral in taste.

rows: Porous carbon pellets trap moisture and tar

r.x: A filtered pipe can also be smoked without the filter; because the empty chamber can increase condensation in that case, using an adapter (reducer) is common.
Systems Built into the Body

The oldest and best-known structural solution is the Peterson System, for which Charles Peterson, one of the founders of Peterson, filed a patent application in 1890 (British-Irish patent 1891, U.S. patent 1894). In the system, the airway is drilled higher than usual; the moisture that condenses collects in a wide reservoir carved into the shank-to-bowl joint. This is complemented by a graduated bore that narrows the airway from the tenon toward the lip, and a P-Lip stem that directs smoke toward the palate rather than the tongue. According to a 1987 advertisement from the company, the graduated bore lets the draw weaken fifteenfold by the time it reaches the tobacco chamber; this figure, however, is an advertising claim rather than a technical measurement.

On the American side, Kaywoodie's screw-in aluminum condenser (the "stinger"), introduced in 1931 as "Drinkless," was the best-known example of a metal device. The Falcon, designed in 1936 by Indiana engineer Kenly Bugg, is a modular system: an interchangeable briar bowl screws onto an aluminum shank-and-bowl base; moisture collects in the "humidome" cup beneath the bowl; the bowl can be unscrewed even mid-smoke to empty the cup. The brand moved into wide production in the late 1940s, and according to company figures it had sold six million units in the U.S. alone by 1954; production moved to England in 1961.
The Debate and Maintenance

The filter question is one of the pipe community's ongoing debates: proponents cite a drier, lighter smoke, opponents cite lost flavor and increased draw resistance, and both traditions are considered well established. Manufacturer claims that filters reduce harmful substances have not been confirmed by independent studies. Maintenance is simple: an activated-carbon filter is discarded after every smoke, while a balsa filter can be dried and reused for several smokes. In system pipes, the moisture that collects in the reservoir should be removed with a tissue while the pipe is still warm, and the pipe should spend the night disassembled into its parts; for general principles, see the pipe cleaning and care entry.

r.x: Antique meerschaum pipes

are pipes hand-carved in Central European workshops roughly throughout the 19th century and into the first quarter of the 20th, most fitted with amber mouthpieces. In collecting, this group is considered a field entirely separate from briar pipes: the evaluation criterion is not smoking performance but the quality and subject of the carving and the pipe's original case.
The Vienna Axis

The first records of meerschaum's use in pipe making reach back to the early 18th century. The often-told story of a Hungarian shoemaker, dated to 1723, is today treated with caution; lacking documentary support, it is a story researchers regard with skepticism. What can be verified is that raw stone extracted from the deposits around Eskişehir was sent to Europe to be worked. Early carving is reported to have concentrated around Pest, with the center soon shifting to Vienna; this city is cited as the field's international center throughout the 19th century. Paris, Berlin, Brussels, and Hungarian workshops were also part of the same network. For the domestic branch of this production, see the Eskişehir meerschaum carving and Tophane pipe making entries.

Some sources give the range 1850-1910, others 1850-1920, but the period from the mid-19th century to the first quarter of the 20th is considered the golden age of antique meerschaum. Carvers worked with a broad repertoire of subjects, from hunting scenes to mythology, from portraits of rulers to opera heroes; custom figures made to commission were also produced. Mouthpieces were mostly amber; much of the amber worked in European workshops of the period was Baltic in origin. Amber's fragility and increasing scarcity led to it being replaced in the 20th century by materials such as hard rubber and acrylic.
Distinguishing Features

Most antique pieces are carved from block meerschaum, that is, from a whole nodule rather than by pressing. As block stone is used, it acquires a patina running from white to yellow, from yellow to reddish brown; this coloring is, for collectors, both an aesthetic and a documenting data point. For the material's general properties, see the meerschaum entry.

In dating, the most practical criterion is the place of production. Türkiye, in a decision widely dated to 1970, banned the export of raw block meerschaum, permitting only worked product to leave the country; some sources place the ban more broadly in the 1970s. This decision effectively ended the European carving craft; subsequent production concentrated largely in Eskişehir. So a figural pipe made in a Vienna or German workshop, as a rule, dates to before 1970.
Collecting Framework

In this field, the case, the stamp, and the carving style are read together. Original velvet- or silk-lined cases are considered part of the piece's integrity. Some of the very small-scale figural examples are not pipes but cigar holders; this distinction is often overlooked in classification. The field's most consulted body of foreign-language work is the writing and books signed Ben Rapaport, who has devoted decades to the subject. Why antique and briar collecting form two separate cultures is discussed in a separate entry.

r.x: Briar curing

is the collective name for the drying and purifying processes a briar burl goes through from the moment it's dug from the ground to the point it becomes a block ready for working. It appears in English sources as
curing

. The purpose is twofold: to remove the sap, resin, and other residues inside the wood, and to keep the remaining moisture balanced at a level low enough not to crack, yet not so high as to spoil the cut. A block whose curing was left incomplete behaves unreliably on the lathe and gives a hot, harsh taste when smoked; curing is therefore considered the least visible stage that determines a briar pipe's quality.
Stages at the Sawmill

When the burl comes out of the ground, the wood is still alive; curing's first job is to kill it without letting it crack. Because sudden drying opens splits, burls are covered with branches or damp soil as they're transported, so that moisture is drawn out slowly. At the sawmill, the same principle is maintained under controlled conditions; burls placed in pits and covered with sacking are reportedly left in this state for roughly three months.

The dead burl is then cut into blocks with large circular saws. Because the dry outer layer can chip on contact with the blade, the surface is wetted just before cutting; the direction of the first cut is the maker's most careful decision, since it determines how many usable blocks the burl will yield. The separated blocks are sorted by size and by whether they come from the bark-covered outer layer or the interior.

The real purification happens through boiling: wood boiled sack by sack releases most of its sap and resin and takes on water in its place. Blocks whose surface has dried are then graded more closely. Grading is largely subjective, because what's inside a block cannot be known until it's cut, and the criteria have also shifted over time. Today bark-covered plateaux is treated as the top grade, whereas Alfred Dunhill Ltd's 1928 encyclopedia
About Smoke

named the wood from the center of the root as the most prized section. Most sources report that blocks are left to dry for roughly another year and a half before being considered ready for sale, though in practice this period can be shortened depending on the buyer's urgency or the workshop's need for cash.
Three Curing Methods
Once a block reaches a workshop, processing continues in different ways.
Air curing:

Blocks are stacked on wire racks in the workshop and typically left for three to five years. It's the oldest and most expensive of the methods; years' worth of briar stock sits on the shelf as capital. The blocks need to be turned occasionally for even drying.
Kiln drying:

Blocks are dried at a controlled temperature; the time is measured in days or weeks rather than years. Regular turning is essential here too, otherwise a block drying faster on one face than the other will split. Some don't count this as a curing method at all, viewing it merely as a way to make the wood workable quickly.
Oil curing:

The method developed by Dunhill founder Alfred Dunhill was filed with the US Patent Office on October 14, 1918; the patent is reported to have been granted in 1920. The rationale is stated plainly in the patent text: for the oil to fully penetrate the wood's fibers, pipes needed to be stored for twelve months or longer, which meant capital sitting idle on the shelf. In practice, bowls were soaked in an oil bath and then fitted onto brass pins heated by gas flames; over weeks, the oil carried resin and residue to the surface, and this layer was wiped away before it could harden into a crust. The patent also covered removing this crust by sandblasting. Dunhill is said to have abandoned this method in the 1970s, and oil curing is reported to continue today at workshops such as Ashton, Radice, and Ferndown.
Cured and Uncured Pipes

Most pipes on the market receive no additional curing beyond the sawmill stages; the block dries, the body is worked, the stem is fitted, and the pipe is readied for sale. Such a pipe can smoke well or poorly; its taste generally needs a long break-in period to settle. Manufacturers who apply extra curing take on the cost of that waiting period up front. Curing can't be said to guarantee a good smoke; what's accepted is that it removes one of the most common causes of a bad one from the outset. The stages by which a block becomes a pipe are covered in the article on how a pipe is made.

r.x: Sandblasting

is the process of propelling fine abrasive particles at a surface with compressed air or suction. In pipe making it's known not to be a simple finishing step: two stummels from the same workshop can look wildly different depending on the machine used, the type of abrasive, the wood's grain, and the habits of the hand at the bench.
From Industry to the Pipe Bench

The method wasn't invented for pipes. Benjamin Chew Tilghman registered sandblasting in the United States on 18 October 1870 under patent No. 108,408; the document covered cutting and etching stone, metal, and glass, with wood not yet on the agenda. He is said to have hit on the idea after watching desert wind-blown sand frost glass surfaces — a story that itself appears in sources with a caveat of legend. Real industrial uptake came only after compressed air was added to the setup in 1904.

Bringing the technique to the pipe took another generation. Dunhill had moved pipe production to its facility at Notting Hill Gate in London in 1916. The first filing for the British patent on the Shell Briar finish (No. 1484/17) was submitted 13 October 1917, completed 12 April 1918, and granted on 14 October of that same year; the American patent followed in 1920, the Canadian in 1921. Documentation of the finish's earliest years consists largely of this patent record; sandblasted pipes are absent from period catalogs and advertisements.
Abrasive and Machine

The first factor shaping the surface is what grain meets the wood. Silica sand, garnet, glass beads, steel shot, crushed steel, walnut shell, and crushed fruit pits are all common abrasives; each leaves a different depth and texture, and a material that gives the right result in one workshop may not meet expectations in another. Silica sand has been banned in the United Kingdom, Germany, Belgium, Sweden, and Russia because of the risk of silicosis.

On the machine side there are two basic setups. In suction (vacuum) cabinets, particles are drawn to the nozzle by suction not exceeding one atmosphere; most small workshop machines work this way. In pressure-pot machines, the abrasive is fed from a sealed vessel under compressed air, the flow is far more forceful, and the pressure can be raised as far as the compressor and plumbing allow — deep relief requires exactly this.

How the hand engages also shows in the result. In cabinets with a fixed nozzle, the maker turns the stummel with both hands and switches the flow on and off with a foot pedal; in gun-style setups, one hand holds the stummel while the other directs the nozzle. In automated setups, a large batch of stummels is tumbled for hours in a wire drum while a fixed nozzle blasts at low pressure. Because the pieces rub against each other in the drum, edges round off and the texture softens; a sandblast with sharp, distinct edges is therefore taken to have been worked by hand.
Grain, Curing, and Depth

The depth of the relief depends largely on the briar block itself. Curing's effect on this is disputed: makers don't agree on which of air-drying, kiln-drying, oil curing, steaming, or soaking in water improves a sandblast; some argue their own method makes a clear difference, others report seeing no difference at all in their own trials. Ashton's practice of steaming a cured bowl to raise the soft grain before blasting is one known example of this search.

The direction of the grain also shows up in the pattern. It's reported that until the early 1960s sawmills cut without regard for grain, leaving plenty of cross- and mixed-grain blocks in circulation — blocks said to give more intricate blast patterns. As Italian and Danish makers gained influence, cutting shifted toward straight grain, which in turn brought out ring patterns more prominently on sandblasted surfaces.
Flaw or Preference

It's a common misconception that a sandblasted pipe was made from a flawed stummel. Until the 1930s, smooth pipes were mostly stained in shades of burgundy or dark walnut, so small sand marks stayed hidden under the stain. The spread of light natural finishes made these marks visible and pushed sandblasting into wider use. Shedding excess weight from the stummel, or hiding a stain that couldn't be applied evenly on a smooth surface, are also cited among the reasons for the choice. For a comparison with other finishes, see surface finishes.

r.x: The hundred-year-old briar

is a widespread claim, passed down through generations in the pipe community, that treats the age of the root burl a pipe block came from as a measure of superiority. Of uncertain origin, the phrase turns up both in manufacturer marketing and in collector correspondence; on the other hand, a significant number of woodworking-literate makers reject it outright. The debate opens onto the question of what actually determines briar quality.
Where the Number Comes From

The hundred-year figure has no single point of origin; it has been fed by more than one channel within the community. One of the best-known examples is a dealer's letter: according to the record, Comoy's of London wrote to the first owner of a six-pipe set it made in 1977, stating that the root used came from the mountains of Greece and had grown there for more than a hundred years. Statements of this kind have become a stock way of giving individual pipes a special backstory.
A second channel is popular publications on the subject. As it's commonly cited, drawing on Richard Carleton Hacker's 2000 book
Pipesmoking: A 21st Century Guide

, the age of the burl worked is said to have dropped step by step over the decades, falling to around fifteen years in cheap production. This declining sequence has, over time, become the basis for the belief that "old pipes were made from better wood."

Both channels share the same weakness: the figures rest on assertion, not measurement. Since the age of an extracted root burl can't be reliably read from annual rings, verifying the age claims circulating in the market is, in practice, impossible.
Barbi's Counter-Argument

The community's most cited counter-argument belongs to maker Rainer Barbi, who worked in Germany from 1974 until his death in 2011. It's reported that in a 2001 magazine column, Barbi addressed the topic under the heading "the hundred-year legend" and treated the claim as a tale with no serious basis. The same piece is said to have given thirty to fifty years as the suitable range for working a root, pointing to climate and soil conditions rather than age as the true determinant of quality.
This range also matches the harvest age given in botanical sources:
Erica arborea

burls are generally recorded as being extracted and cured for long periods at thirty to sixty years of age. The ages implied by praise for "old briar," then, fall well outside the usual harvest window.
What Gets Judged Instead of Age

In practice, what determines a block's value is not how many years the tree grew but how it grew. The soil structure and rainfall pattern that allow the burl to develop at a steady rate largely determine the grain pattern later visible on the surface. The curing stage after extraction is a second, independent threshold; even a good burl that's poorly dried can become unusable.

For this reason most makers who select blocks look not at claimed age but at the texture of the cut surface, the weight of the block, and flaws such as cracks, pith rot, or sand pits. The phrase "hundred-year-old briar" is today regarded less as a measurable trait than as a marketing line.

r.x: Trever Talbert's drilling method

is a workshop practice describing on which machine and in what order the three holes in a briar body — mortise, airway, and tobacco chamber — are opened. By his own account, Talbert has been making pipes since the mid-1990s; after a stretch of seven years working on France's west coast, he returned to the United States. The routine described below is understood to reflect the practice settled on at his workshop in Brittany, as recorded. The brand's overall history is covered in the Talbert Pipes entry.
Why the Lathe

Drilling is considered the least forgiving step in pipe making: once the bore drifts off axis, the body usually can't be saved. The reasons for preferring a lathe over a drill press cluster around this risk. A bit fed by the tailstock keeps feeding information to the maker's hand continuously; this is how a crack inside the wood, or the moment the bit breaks through into the airway, is sensed by feel rather than sight. The wide, flat bits used to open the chamber tend to bounce and oval out the hole on a drill press, while they run true on a lathe; the reduced vibration also leaves the hole's surface smoother. On the other hand, the lathe needs to be set up anew for every body: the headstock takes a heavy, two-jawed chuck forged specifically for pipe making, and the tailstock takes a drill chuck. The lathe's general use in the workshop is detailed further in the metal lathe and drilling on a lathe entries.
Order and Speed

The location and depth of the chamber are marked on the block beforehand; the body is mounted in the chuck by the flat surfaces deliberately left on its underside during shaping. Because these flats serve as the reference for every alignment that follows, the shape is given before drilling; the reasoning is discussed in the shaping before drilling entry. The mortise is drilled first, then the airway, adjusting the angle if needed. Once the body is turned in the chuck and the chamber's axis is aligned with the airway, work moves on to the chamber; which chamber bit to use is decided at the design stage.

Speed is kept low; the source gives this limit as the machine's lowest gear, 500 rpm. At high speed the bit bounces, heat builds up, and the wood can scorch. This is why the bit is advanced slowly, withdrawn often to clear chips, and given time to cool. Since the odds of hard wood pushing the bit off axis increase the further it gets from the tailstock, feed is done in short steps. Once the airway is reached, the remaining distance to the base is measured, and the drilling continues by that same amount so the chamber base sits evenly.
The Saint-Claude Machine

The lathe isn't the only option; the workshop is reported to also have several other machines built specifically for pipe making, alongside drill presses. One of these is a drilling machine made in Saint-Claude. The block is clamped into self-centering jaws mounted vertically; a carriage rides toward the bit, which is chucked to a heavy steel spindle turned from overhead by a belt. Because the carriage can rise and fall, slide sideways, and swivel through a thirty-degree arc relative to the source, the chamber and the airway can be opened without loosening the block. The jaws are used with soft wooden blocks softer than the briar itself: they grip firmly but harmlessly and are replaced as they wear. The workshop's larger machines are recorded as applying the same principle with horizontally mounted jaws.

r.x: The American sandblasting school

is a collective heading used to sum up the debate that ran through the 2000s over whether the level American independent pipe makers reached in sandblast surfaces amounted to a distinct school of its own. One of the texts that gave the debate visibility is Fred Hanna's 2008 piece in
The Pipe Collector

, the bulletin of the North American Society of Pipe Collectors. The society's origins trace to a collector circle in Ohio; records show it was founded in 1993 as the Ohio Pipe Collectors and took its current name in 1997. The bulletin is a regular publication gathering member articles and maker interviews.
The Subject of the Debate

Sandblasting is a surface treatment that erodes the soft summer rings of briar and leaves the hard winter rings standing in relief; its details are covered in the art of sandblasting entry. The method's established reference point in pipe making is Alfred Dunhill's Shell finish, based on a patent he filed for in 1917 and received in 1918. Hanna's claim is that the standard shifted in the following generation, and that, looking across countries and brands, the deepest and most detailed surfaces now came from independent American makers. The technical distinction the piece rests on is that sandblasting stops being a fix reached for to cover a flaw in the wood and becomes a surface language in its own right, one that renders the grain pattern legible.
Makers Named

The seven workshops cited in the piece are given below in surname order; what they share is that they treat sandblasting not as a single-pass preparatory step but as a stage worked on in its own right.
Paul Bonacquisti

— Grew up immersed in woodworking in North Greenbush, near Albany, New York; took up pipe making seriously in 1994 and exhibited for the first time in 1996. He names his sandblasted finish "Sabbia" as a distinct grade of its own.
J. T. Cooke

— Working in Vermont, Cooke turned to pipe repair and then pipe making after leaving his role as art director at WCAX television in 1976. Around 1999 he developed a multi-stage sandblasting routine that grew to five stages; nearly all of the pipes he produces carry sandblasted surfaces.
John Eells

— The son of a tool-and-die-maker father, Eells was known within the Conclave of Richmond Pipe Smokers (CORPS) circle; he was noted for interpreting classic shapes at above-average dimensions. He passed away in 2022.
Larry Roush

— Working in Ohio, Roush came to pipe making by way of jewelry-making; he first fitted his own silver and gold bands to pipes he collected, then began making his own pipes in the 1990s. He added sandblasting to his workshop relatively late.
Brian Ruthenberg
— The name with the least independent record among those listed; promotional texts point to a machinist and woodworking background and a limited number of pipes produced per year.
Trever Talbert
— After winning the carving competition
Pipes & Tobaccos
magazine first held in 1997, he made the craft his profession; he settled in France in May 2002 and works with bog oak (morta) alongside briar.
Lee von Erck
— Works in Negaunee, in Michigan's Upper Peninsula; known for the porous "morel" surface he achieves through sandblasting.
Limits of the Assessment

The piece states an opinion, not a measurement; Hanna himself notes that individually superior examples can be found from brands such as Dunhill or Ashton. A second debate that circles around the text is whether multi-stage deep sandblasting edges toward rustication; some collectors have used the description "sand-carved" for these surfaces. Hanna pushes back against the label, arguing that the erosion does not produce an artificial texture but exposes the wood's own ring structure. The relationship between the level of detail and the labor spent is also frequently noted: the piece reports that Cooke devotes twelve to fifteen hours to sandblasting alone on a single pipe, while promotional material published in later years speaks of a total of twenty-four to forty hours for one pipe. By which criteria different surface finishes are to be compared remains the still-open side of this debate.

r.x: The asbestos pipe

is a bowl material that emerged in the last quarter of the 19th century and was entirely abandoned about a generation later. It was made either by molding asbestos fiber with a binder or by applying it as a lining inside a bowl made of another material; it stood in tobacconists' display cases alongside briar, meerschaum, and clay pipes. Today it is given very little space in pipe-history narratives.
Asbestos's Years of Prestige

Named from an Ancient Greek word meaning "unquenchable," asbestos was industry's favorite material in the second half of the 19th century: insulation, fire curtains, brake linings, machine gaskets. Mining that began in the 1870s at the Thetford deposits in Quebec, Canada, made the fiber both more abundant and cheaper within a few decades. With a fire-resistant, lightweight raw material that took whatever shape was wanted readily at hand, it is not surprising that pipe makers tried it.

The first record of the danger dates to the same years. The 1898 annual report of the Chief Inspector of Factories and Workshops in Great Britain, based on the observations of Lucy Deane Streatfeild, one of the first female factory inspectors, documented the harm of asbestos dust. By contrast, the first description of the disease in medical literature came only in 1924, and the first British regulation aimed at the asbestos industry was published in 1931.
The Jackson Patent and English Production

According to period patent indexes, the first person to register the asbestos pipe was Charles Jackson, holder of British patent no. 1453 dated 20 March 1883. The registration covered both asbestos pipes with or without a mouthpiece and the placing of an asbestos lining in the shank of a pipe made of another material. Records show production was carried on under the name Jackson Asbestos Manufacturing Company in Nottingham and Birmingham, the products appeared at the 1888-1889 Melbourne Centennial Exhibition, and won a medal at an exhibition held in Birmingham. Period records also show the firm advertising in 1909 its raw material as "the finest Canadian asbestos fiber."
Against this confident advertising language, one of the period's asbestos handbooks, Robert H. Jones's
Asbestos and Asbestic

, gives a far more measured account of the trade's actual course. According to the book, the material's only real advantage was lightness; the high sales of the early years declined once it became clear the bowl heated up uncomfortably. It is also reported that Jackson himself acknowledged in later years that the bowl softened with extended use.
Traces on the Continent and in America

The material took hold on the European continent in factories that came out of the clay-pipe tradition. In Belgium, the De Bevere family's workshop in Kortrijk produced asbestos pipes alongside fired clay; in 1930 it dropped clay pipes and continued with briar and asbestos. The J. J. Knoedgen factory in Bree, founded in 1846 and changing hands in 1979, followed the same path.

The same idea found an echo across the Atlantic too. US patent no. 549,418, granted 5 November 1895 to Ambrose W. Woodward of Lancaster, Pennsylvania, describes mixing asbestos and plaster in a dextrin solution and applying it as a lining to the inner surface of the bowl. Albert Angell of Orange, New Jersey, in patent no. 783,394 registered on 21 February 1905, proposed coating strips of asbestos paper with condensed milk and forming them into a tube shape, then hardening the result at high heat. Toronto's William W. Hesson, in patent no. 1,455,396 granted 15 May 1923, kneaded four measures of ground corncob with one measure of asbestos fiber, a small amount of plant fiber, and a binder.

The material's dark appearance was recognized well enough to be imitated: a British patent taken out in the 1890s describes first passing clay pipes through a smoky firing and then glazing them to give the impression of meerschaum, briar, or asbestos pipes. Asbestos also entered pipes even where it was not the bowl material. Dunhill, in the GB 213,855 patent it filed on 13 November 1923, described a thin, perforated asbestos disc pressed onto packed tobacco to prevent ash from scattering in the wind and to stop the tobacco burning too fast.
Why It Disappeared

The asbestos pipe quietly withdrew from the market after the first quarter of the 20th century. The reason that stands out in the trade press of the period is not health but usage discomfort: the bowl heated up more than expected and degraded with prolonged use. Looking back today, the more striking point is different: these pipes show how easily a mineral whose harm was already on record in those very years could find its way into an everyday object. How bowl material preference changed over time is treated together in the pipe bowl materials entry.

r.x: The Kaldenberg Company

was the most visible of the firms manufacturing meerschaum pipes in New York during the second half of the 19th century. The small turning and ornament workshop founded by German immigrant Frederick William Kaldenberg grew, under the hand of his son Frederick Julius Kaldenberg, into a seven-story factory with branches in four cities and one of the era's most ambitious advertising campaigns. The same firm fell apart before the century ended. Records list it under the names F. W. Kaldenberg, Kaldenberg & Son, and F. J. Kaldenberg Co. in turn.
From Turner's Workshop to Factory

The exact founding year is uncertain; records give 1853, 1855, and 1858. The commonly accepted account is that the workshop, established in 1853 for amber, ivory, and mother-of-pearl work, moved into meerschaum pipe-making in 1855. A New York city directory from 1865 still describes the firm as a turner and ornament craftsman, at an address near Broadway on John Street. As the story goes, what drew the founder into this line was an encounter with a merchant named Bedrossian who had brought two crates of raw stone from Anatolia; because the story isn't backed by a contemporary document, it's cited with caution. The era's raw stone trade was entirely dependent on the Eskişehir deposits.

When the son became a partner in the business in 1867, the sign became "Kaldenberg & Son"; two years later, management passed entirely to Frederick Julius. As the firm grew it both relocated and diversified: after the factory and salesroom on Fulton Street, it moved to a seven-story facility on East 33rd Street, and branches opened in Boston, Philadelphia, Chicago, and St. Louis. The catalog didn't stay limited to pipes; amber stems, ivory goods, billiard balls, and canes were added to the list. By the late 1870s, some seventy-five people were working at the New York workshop, at least forty of them dedicated solely to the meerschaum department; most of the craftsmen were immigrants who had learned the trade in Europe.
Exhibition Awards and Advertising Language

Pipe manufacturers began appearing at international exhibitions starting with the 1851 London Great Exhibition; American manufacturers only stepped onto this stage in the 1860s. Kaldenberg & Son entered the Paris Universal Exposition, held April 1 - October 31, 1867, with thirty pipes, and was the only firm among the six American entrants in the fancy-goods class to receive an award. The nature of the award differs by source: the official report of the American commissioners calls it an honorable mention, while some later accounts speak of a bronze medal. At the Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia in 1876, the international jury reserved the single award given to American-made meerschaum goods for Kaldenberg; the showpiece brought to the exhibition was a four-stemmed piece over seventy centimeters tall, topped with a figure of Columbia. Medals also came from the American Institute exhibitions in New York in 1866, 1870, and 1874.

These awards were endlessly repeated in advertisements. The Paris honorable mention was presented for years as "an award won competing against the whole world"; the firm did not shy from billing itself as the country's only true meerschaum manufacturer and the largest in the world. In the same years, its main rival, William Demuth & Co., known for the WDC stamp inside a triangle, ran almost no advertising at all.
Patented Designs

Frederick Julius Kaldenberg's name is documented by two patents. U.S. Patent 90,554, dated May 25, 1869, describes a cup of raw, porous meerschaum that sits inside the chamber without touching it: the cup absorbs the tobacco's moisture before it reaches the chamber, and a saucer at its base collects any excess moisture. The aim was to prevent moisture from clogging the stone's pores and weakening the body; the document also describes a mouth opening that directs smoke upward. This is most likely the "patented pipe" the firm advertised in 1869. On March 16, 1886, a design patent was taken for a shank with a diamond-shaped cross-section; in this document, Kaldenberg's address is given as Tarrytown.
Collapse and Dispersal

In May 1887, the business was incorporated with five hundred thousand dollars in capital; well-known names such as pencil manufacturer Eberhard Faber joined its board. The financial panic of 1893 halted this expansion: a tightening money market, slowing collections, and the failure of an indebted European customer combined, and Kaldenberg made an assignment for the benefit of creditors in early April; the factory building was sold that same year, and manufacturing continued afterward on leased premises. The Kaldenberg Pipe Company, founded in 1896, lost its factory to a fire that broke out on Christmas Day of that year and never recovered; F. J. Kaldenberg's personal bankruptcy petition was accepted on November 1, 1900. He himself died in 1912 at his home in Tarrytown. By this time the market had shifted to briar, and no successor firm carrying the Kaldenberg name ever matched its 19th-century standing.

r.x: Tagua
is the name given to the ripened seed of ivory palms (genus
Phytelephas

) that grow in the tropical forests of South America. When the nutritive tissue inside the seed dries, it hardens like stone and takes on a matte white, faintly veined surface. This appearance is what earned the material the name "vegetable ivory." In the pipe world, tagua is known less as a bowl material than as one used for ornamentation and shank extensions.
Source and Properties of the Material

The ivory palm is found chiefly in Ecuador, in the rainforests along the western slopes of the Andes. The tree can take up to fifteen years to bear its first fruit; once mature, it goes on bearing fruit for decades. Inside the large, hard-shelled fruit clusters borne by female trees are seeds several centimeters across, arranged in rows. An unripe seed is soft and edible in texture; hardness only emerges over the drying process.

Once dried, the seed becomes too resistant to carve with a knife; working it requires a saw, files, and sandpaper. On the other hand, it lends itself well to cutting, drilling, and polishing to a high gloss; in this respect its behavior on the bench resembles animal ivory. Because dye only penetrates the outer layer, colored pieces show the white core in contrast with the darker surface. Records indicate it became one of the main raw materials for the button industry starting in the 1880s, a use that largely declined as plastic spread.
Use in Pipes

Tagua's most common function in a pipe is as the shank extension or decorative band placed between the shank and the stem. A seed no more than a few centimeters across is often not suited to producing a full-length pipe body; but it's more than enough for a thin band or a short extension. The contrast the white surface creates against dark briar and black vulkanit is what draws makers who choose the material for ornamentation. Even so, the number of makers who use tagua is limited, and the material isn't counted among the main materials in pipe making.

In Ecuador, local craftsmen are known to carve small pipes by hollowing out a whole tagua seed: the top of the seed is opened into a bowl shape, and a channel is drilled from inside toward the stem. These are mostly figural, souvenir-grade pieces. Being a plant-based tissue, the material isn't expected to withstand sustained burning heat as well as briar or meerschaum; in this respect tagua repeats a pattern seen in most bowl materials other than briar: an eye-catching surface, a limited service life.

The material's current appeal isn't just about looks. Growing sensitivity toward the trade in animal ivory has made tagua a well-regarded alternative. The seeds are collected from fallen fruit without harming the tree; this commercial value also helps keep the palm standing in areas cleared for agriculture. The Ecuadorian ivory palm is currently listed as "near threatened" by the IUCN.

r.x: Olive wood pipes

is the name given to pipes made from the wood of the olive tree (Olea europaea), the emblem of the Mediterranean basin. Among woods other than briar, it's one of the most widely used; thanks to both its hardness and its visibly striking grain pattern, it has long been a material pipe makers turn to.
Material Properties

The olive tree grows very slowly and can live for centuries; the trunk diameter thickens only over many years. This slow growth gives the wood a dense, hard structure. Wood reference data typically give its specific gravity at 12% moisture as roughly 0.98, with a unit weight of around 980 kg/m³; its Janka hardness is around 2,700 lbf, a value that places olive among the upper tier of hardwoods. The grain can be straight, or it can be intricate and irregular; the texture is fine, evenly distributed, and gives a surface with a measured natural sheen. Curved, wavy, or burl-like patterns are common, and this pattern differs markedly from the regular lines sought in briar grain.

As lumber, olive isn't abundant through commercial channels. Since healthy trees are kept for their fruit, the material that reaches workshops mostly comes from pruning waste, broken branches, or diseased orchard trees. This limits block size and makes larger-bowled shapes difficult.
Behavior in Pipe Making

Olive wood turns very well on the lathe and takes on a strong sheen when polished. On the other hand, the drying stage is troublesome: the material is prone to cracking and warping, and its dimensional stability is low. This makes long, controlled drying of the block, and careful attention to the curing and processing stage, all the more important. Tear-out can occur when working the surface of intricately grained pieces, which is why patiently working through the sanding grits matters here. Because the wood's oil content is high, glue joints can be strained in some pieces; makers commonly key or channel the surfaces where a shank extension or a ring is added.
Comparison with Briar

Although olive wood isn't as easy to find as briar, it's among the best-known alternatives in the pipe community, and it's generally discussed under the heading pipes in woods other than briar. According to common opinion in the community, the fundamental difference between the two materials lies in heat behavior: briar's porous root structure is said to dissipate heat more comfortably, while olive wood is said to heat up faster; for this reason olive bowls are considered to call for a slow, steady puffing pace. It's also often noted that new pipes can show a faint woody taste in early bowls, which fades as a cake builds up inside the bowl. Both points are observations circulating in maker and user forums rather than findings from a comparative measurement.

In terms of color, olive spans a range from honeyed yellow tones to dark brown veining. Since the natural pattern differs in every piece, no two olive wood pipes look alike. For the same reason, the material is cited among alternative woods used in pipe making as an option prized for its aesthetics.

r.x: Hydrostone and resin pipes

describes pipes produced by mold-casting, standing outside the carved tradition of briar and meerschaum. What ties the two materials together is a shared production logic: a mold reproduces every detail of a fine carving as many times as wanted, without further labor. This convenience produced two very different outcomes in pipe making. Plaster-based hydrostone remained an openly declared copying and repair material; resin, meanwhile, became both the raw material of cheap mass-produced bowls and the chief tool of forgery in the collector market.
Hydrostone: A Copy in Plaster

Hydrostone is the trade name of a high-strength plaster used in American casting and model-making industries. The chemical basis of the plaster is calcium sulfate hemihydrate; it begins to set about ten minutes after being mixed with water, completes its initial hardening within an hour, and continues to gain strength over the following days as its internal crystal structure changes. Because it sets into a white, tight-grained, lightweight mass, it's favored for sculpture, figurines, and mold work. These same qualities also make it well suited to imitating meerschaum's matte white surface.

The period this material is associated with pipes is the early 1970s. Records show that Michael Seiden, who bought and sold antique meerschaum pipes in Cambridge, Massachusetts, advertised hydrostone castings of pipes and cigar holders from his own collection in Hobbies magazine in the fall of 1971. These pieces were sold as copies, not fakes, and weren't intended to be smoked either. That's also what made the experiment short-lived: plaster isn't a bowl material that can stand up to fire. It does, however, still come to mind as a filler in repairing a cracked meerschaum bowl.
Resin Enters Pipe Making

Resin is a solid or very thick substance, of plant or synthetic origin, capable of being turned into a polymer. It entered pipe making first through the mouthpiece; the early 20th century's gutta-percha and Redmanol examples are where early phenolic resins were first tried. In the bowl, the best-known formulation is Brylon: S. M. Frank & Co. developed this material in 1966, combining resin with wood flour to give a cheap alternative to briar, and began producing part of its Medico and Yello-Bole lines from it. Both brands still carry Brylon models today. Among smokers, Brylon is known for its low cost and resistance to breakage; it's also criticized for being heavy and smoking hot. Another trial of the same period is the "the pipe" line, produced starting in 1963 by the Super-Temp company, its bowl interior lined with pyrolytic graphite; marketed under the name Venturi after 1965, this line went out of production in the mid-1970s. A comparison of these materials is covered in the article on pipe bowl materials.
Where Copy Ends and Fake Begins

Imitation meerschaum is not a 20th-century invention. In 19th-century English humor writing, reading the word "meerschaum" as "mere sham" was a wordplay that circulated for a time; in the same years, chips of the genuine stone were kneaded with clay into a paste and sold as "artificial meerschaum." Cast resin added a new possibility to this line, because a body coming out of a mold could be marketed as a carved antique. The example the community knows best is a pipe bearing a misspelled "Gustav Fisher Jnr" signature on the bowl and a reference to the 1873 Vienna exhibition on the body. That it was produced from the same mold in large numbers is evident from the piece's repeated reappearance at auctions and online marketplaces; its manufacturer is unknown. It's also reported that resin copies made by an English dealer in the early 2000s, cast from molds taken off his own antique meerschaums, have circulated at auction.
Notes on Telling Them Apart

The signs that give away a cast body generally appear together: a bowl stained dark red from day one to hide the mold seam, crude and detail-poor carving, walls of uniform thickness throughout, a plastic mouthpiece instead of amber, and a cast zinc-alloy band instead of silver. There are also two old criteria the community has repeated for about a century. The first is rubbing the surface with silver: a synthetic body leaves a mark resembling a pencil line, while genuine stone doesn't. The second is color change; imitation material doesn't turn honey-colored with smoking. The problem also isn't confined to a single material: on the briar side, the fake Dunhills of the 1980s describe a similar episode.

r.x: The
band saw

is a cutting machine in which a thin, long blade — welded at both ends into a loop — is stretched and driven between two wheels. It's not counted among the pipe workshop's mandatory machines; drilling and shaping can be carried out without one. Even so, it's regarded as one of the first "convenience" tools that speed up the work: it takes the excess off a square briar block in seconds and noticeably cuts down what's left for sanding or filing. For where cutting fits in the production flow, see the how a pipe is made entry.
Working Principle and Brief History

The machine's idea isn't new: William Newberry was granted a patent in England in 1809 for the concept of cutting with an endless band blade. But the steel of the day couldn't bear the strain, blades kept snapping, and the design remained on paper for a long time. The step that solved the problem came in France in 1846, when Anne Paulin Crepin's welding method was transferred to A. Perin & Company in Paris, and a usable blade emerged along with advances in alloy and tempering technique. America's first band saw patent is recorded as having been granted in 1836 to Benjamin Barker of Ellsworth, Maine.
Blade Width and Turning Radius

On a band saw, the decisive measurement isn't the machine's power but the blade's width. The narrower the blade, the tighter a curve it can follow; as it widens, it becomes more stable in straight cuts and more reluctant to take a curve. Manufacturers' published minimum-radius charts don't line up exactly; the figures given for a 3/8-inch blade range roughly from one to one and a half inches. In pipe making, this width is considered a suitable middle ground: it's enough to take the corners off a block and rough out the outline, and for tighter curves the work is left to sanding anyway. The general rule is to use the widest blade suited to the cut at hand.

The cleanness of the cut depends on setup as much as on the blade. General woodworking practice holds that correctly tensioning the blade, setting the upper and lower guides close to the blade, lowering the guide to the workpiece, and squaring the table keep the cut from drifting off the line. On an unadjusted machine the blade wanders sideways and causes a loss in the block that's hard to make up for.
Place in the Workshop

The band saw's job is limited to rough cutting; the final surface never comes off the saw. Once the block is cut, the work moves on to tools like a belt sander or a lathe. Some makers prefer to cut after drilling the hole, because a square block mounts more securely on a drill press; see the shaping before drilling entry for this preference. Grain direction also matters during cutting: how much is taken from which face of the block directly determines the grain pattern that will show on the outside.

Two points stand out for safety. At least two of the blade's teeth should be in contact with the workpiece at all times; otherwise the teeth can catch and strip. Second is the fine dust briar leaves behind — dust extraction and eye protection are needed at this machine too.

r.x: Mouthpiece materials

cover the substances used to make the mouthpiece (stem), the part of the pipe that touches the lips and carries smoke from the bowl to the mouth. Two main materials stand out in today's pipes: hardened rubber, or ebonite (vulcanite), and acrylic (Lucite). In the past, amber, horn, ivory, and early plastics were common. Material choice determines not just appearance but also comfort against the teeth, maintenance needs, and durability.
Ebonite (Vulcanite)

Ebonite is the product of the vulcanization process Charles Goodyear discovered in 1839: rubber is mixed with a high proportion of sulfur and the mixture hardened by prolonged heating. One of Goodyear's early patents explicitly lists the pipe mouthpiece among suitable applications. The material's three names are synonyms: "ebonite" comes from its resemblance to ebony wood, "vulcanite" from the heat treatment, while the English "hard rubber" refers directly to its meaning.

Ebonite feels soft against the teeth and flexes slightly when bitten; this is why it is preferred by those who hold the pipe clenched in their teeth (clenchers). Its greatest flaw is oxidation: the sulfur it contains migrates to the surface through reaction with light, oxygen, and saliva. A glossy black mouthpiece gradually shifts to a greenish-brown tone and gives off a bitter, chemical taste. To slow oxidation, it is recommended to store the mouthpiece away from light and apply protective oil; see the pipe cleaning and care entry for detail.
Acrylic and Cumberland

Acrylic mouthpieces do not oxidize, require almost no maintenance, and can be produced in any color or with pearlescent or veined patterns. On the other hand they feel harder and more slippery against the teeth, can be prone to brittleness especially around the tenon area, and cannot be cut as thin as ebonite.

r.x: The material called Cumberland (brindle) is colored, swirled ebonite; its classic form has dark red-black veining. The name comes from Dunhill: a two-tone vulcanite mouthpiece was first seen in the Root Briar line in 1930, while the "Cumberland" finish as such was introduced around 1979-80. As the story goes, the name is linked to old pipes found in the firm's warehouse on Cumberland Road in London.
Historical Materials: Amber, Horn, and Early Plastics

Amber, fossilized tree resin, was the standard luxury mouthpiece material during the 19th-century golden age of meerschaum pipes; carved bowls from Vienna and Budapest workshops were accompanied by mouthpieces turned from genuine amber. Both expensive and extremely brittle, this material was abandoned in the 20th century. In Turkish meerschaum pipe making too, the classic pairing was a meerschaum bowl with an amber mouthpiece; amber's place has since largely been taken over by acrylic. Horn, ivory, and bone were common in 19th-century French pipe making; mouthpiece making was often a separate craft from bowl carving.

Amber's principal substitute became bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, patented by Leo Baekeland in 1907; semi-translucent derivatives such as Redmanol were common in the 1920s. Casein-based Galalith, however, could not gain a foothold in pipe mouthpieces because it cracked under prolonged contact with liquid.
Shapes: Profile and Bit Types

Mouthpiece profile splits into two main types: taper, which narrows without interruption from the shank diameter to the lips, and saddle, which narrows sharply at one step and then continues straight. The saddle profile reduces weight and makes gripping with the teeth easier; the taper profile gives a classic, flowing silhouette. Structural details such as how the mouthpiece connects to the bowl via the tenon are covered in the pipe anatomy entry.

On the bit side, the most common type is the fishtail, whose horizontal slot in the flattened end fans the smoke out over the tongue. The main alternative is the P-Lip, patented by Peterson at the end of the 19th century: because the smoke hole is on top, the smoke is directed toward the palate and tongue bite is reduced; on the other hand it makes passing a pipe cleaner through more difficult. The round-holed (orific) bits seen on old pipes remain, today, a historical variant.

r.x: The comparison between
old Dunhill and new Dunhill

is one of the longest-running debates in briar pipe collecting. The claim's essence is simple: pipes bearing early stamps are said to have been made of better wood, and later generations are said not to have reached the same level. The classic text on the subject is the comparison collector and dealer R.D. Field published in Pipe Smoker magazine in the fall of 1983; rather than simply relaying the community's received wisdom, Field addresses the subject by laying out what actually changed in production and when. Over the more than four decades since, the debate hasn't closed.
The Collector's Three Periods

Collectors divide production roughly into three periods. Pipes with a patent number on the shank are considered the "patent era"; records show this practice began in 1905, ended in 1954, and patent numbers weren't used on pipes made after 1955. The second period runs 1955-1968, the third from 1968 onward. On the secondary (estate) market, interest in patent-era examples has always exceeded that shown toward the other two periods. That stamps carry this much weight also explains why detailed Dunhill dating guides have grown into a literature of their own.
The Shift in Briar Sources

In the early period, a separate briar source was set aside for each finish: Italian wood was used for smooth-finish Bruyere and Root, Algerian wood for the sandblasted Shell, Sardinian wood for Tanshell. It's reported that the roots worked averaged sixty to a hundred years of age.

This arrangement broke down in the 1960s. Wood from Algeria became scarce after the country's war of independence (1954-1962); records from the same years also mention that Italy reserved its own briar for domestic manufacturers. The practice of setting aside a single source for one finish thus came to an end, and the firm shifted its emphasis to Greek briar. The new wood was harder, lighter, and more evenly grained; the burls, however, were small and flawed, so wastage rose.
Sandblast and Mouthpiece

The most visible result of the change shows up in the Shell finish, introduced in 1917. The loose texture of Algerian wood, combined with the heat of the firm's oil-curing method, produced deep pits and sharp ridges on the surface. It's reported that in the early years, bodies turned to identical measurements could diverge from one another so much by the end of the process that these pipes weren't even stamped with a shape number. The hardness of Greek wood shallowed the sandblasting; in exchange, bodies coming from the same shape became consistent with one another.

A similar trajectory can be seen on the mouthpiece side as well. Hand-cutting is preferred over factory mold-casting: a piece cut from an ebonite sheet or rod is shaped, and the tenon end is thinned one at a time to fit the shank. The main detail that changed is lip thickness. The thick lip of the earliest examples was thinned and widened in the "comfy" shape in the 1920s, and the "fishtail" was added to this in the 1930s. When labor costs brought machine cutting onto the agenda in 1976, a thick lip reappeared as a result; complaints that followed led to machine cutting being abandoned.
Decline, or Divergence?

Two decisions made about the finishes in the mid-1970s also feed the debate: the Shell was darkened entirely with a bluish-black stain, while the Bruyere was lightened from its original plum tone. It's reported that the Bruyere was returned to its old tone shortly after, and that the darker Shell experiment wasn't well received either; in later years a deeply sandblasted Shell line was reintroduced. Field's assessment is that all these steps were part of a continuous evolution rather than a decline in quality: Dunhill arrived at a different pipe while keeping its own standard. That the debate is still alive confirms as much. The age of the wood, the depth of the sandblast, and the thickness of the lip can each be measured separately; "a sweeter smoke," because it can't be measured, remains a matter of opinion.

r.x: Shaping before drilling

is a workshop method in which a pipe body is shaped before the chamber, airway, and mortise are opened. The usual order is the reverse: the block is mounted on the lathe, the three holes are drilled while the body is still rough, and the shape is then built around those axes. Because reversing the order changes both the design decisions and the workshop routine from the ground up, the method counts as a distinct specialty within pipe making.
Shape Led by the Grain

The rationale is the grain. Both the pattern of a briar block and the sand pits, cracks, and voids within it only become visible as the surface is opened up. If the holes are drilled first, the shape stays tied to those axes; working around a flaw that appears during cutting, or capturing the line where the grain looks best, is only possible within a narrow margin. When the shape comes first, though, the maker can choose a new direction every time the saw and sanding disc reveal a new surface. This is why the method is associated with freehand designs, in which the block itself determines the shape, and with the Danish school tradition. The cost is a narrower margin for correction: while roughing out the shape, care must be taken not to end up with a body that can't be drilled at all, and to leave enough material for fine shaping once drilling is done.
Achieving Alignment

The real challenge is drilling three holes that align with each other in a body whose shape is already finished and curved; since the body can no longer be mounted properly on the lathe, drilling is largely done by hand. In practice, the body is marked out first: a laser level stands in for a straightedge, marking the line that bisects the body across its curved surfaces along with the axes of the chamber, mortise, and airway. The points where these lines intersect become the anchor points for drilling; a small piece of briar or a drop of epoxy glued at each intersection both protects the surface and firms up the anchor. During drilling, the bit is chucked to the headstock spindle and turns while the body is held by hand; a sharpened guide pin fitted to the tailstock supports the body at the marked point to keep the axis true. The chamber is widened in stages with custom-made bits after a thin pilot hole is drilled first. Those describing the method specifically note that this stage is dangerous and should not be attempted without proper tools and experience. Once drilling is finished, the shank face is trued so it sits exactly perpendicular to the mortise; only then is the stem shaped and fitted to the body, with fine shaping continuing on both together. The parts and how they fit together are described in the pipe anatomy entry.
Names Who Passed the Method On

Todd Johnson played a large part in spreading the method through American workshops. Johnson began pipe making in the spring of 2000, learned the shape-first, freehand-drill routine from Tom Eltang in the winter of 2001, and then worked with Lars Ivarsson to deepen his understanding of Danish shaping. The method's workshop details were put into writing by Scott E. Thile — a piano technician in Murray, Kentucky, who began pipe making in 2004 — in notes transcribed to Pipedia in 2011; Thile states that he learned most of the practice from Johnson. The idea of using a laser level on curved surfaces is credited to Jack Howell, who began pipe making in 1999, sold his first pipe in 2004, and plays bass clarinet in the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra; the idea of gluing a piece of briar at intersection points is credited to maker John Crosby. The custom chamber bits used are the work of Brad Pohlmann, who comes from a four-year tool-and-die apprenticeship and makes most of his own tools.

r.x: The
discovery of briar

is one of the most debated questions in pipe history. That briar was adopted as a pipe material in the mid-19th century is certain; who first tried it, where, and in what year is not. No registry entry or patent survives. Every known claim was written down decades after the fact, and mostly at second hand; the sections below should therefore be read not as established facts but as competing clusters of narrative.
The Corsica Account
The most widely repeated account rests on Alfred Dunhill's 1924 pipe history,
The Pipe Book

. According to this story, a French pipe manufacturer traveling to Napoleon's birth island had his meerschaum pipe break, had a local peasant make him a new one from briar, and brought samples of the material back with him. Dunhill's son, Alfred Henry Dunhill, continued the same line in his 1954 book; in 1962, American manufacturer Carl B. Weber repeated a simplified version of the story in his own pipe guide. No document has ever been produced to support this account, and the date given is only a loose range, something like "the early 1850s." That all three books reached wide readerships has made this the best-known version of the story, independent of its documentary value.
Traces Leading to the Beaucaire Fair

French sources look elsewhere: to the Madeleine fair held every year from July 15 to 25 at Beaucaire, on the banks of the Rhône. Founded in 1217 and considered France's most crowded trade gathering for centuries, this fair had lost much of its former weight with the spread of the railway; even so, the encounters described in the sources take place here. In 1929, geographer André Mathieu wrote that a turner returning from the fair in 1854 thought to try briar in a pipe. In 1937, Thérèse Colin reported that a craftsman from Saint-Claude received the same suggestion, also in 1854, from a southern merchant he met at the fair. Two further claims later entered the literature: that delegates Regad and Buat of the Saint-Claude Chamber of Arts and Manufactures were inspired by a hardwood salt cellar they saw at an inn, and that a turner named David from Chaumont brought the first samples to the town. Both remain undated claims passed down from generation to generation.
Ligier's Testimony

The most detailed account in terms of date and place entered the literature through André Paul Bastien's 1973 book. Bastien relays the testimony of Jules Ligier, who worked at a Saint-Claude trading house of the period: in the first days of October 1858, a southern merchant named Taffanel, arriving at the Gay Aîné shop to sell boxwood logs, pulled from his pocket a roughly six-sided pipe with a bamboo mouthpiece, cut with a saw. According to the merchant, the pipe was made of briar, and a shepherd from his own region had smoked it for over a year without the wood burning through. According to Ligier, an order for roughly 1,440 rough blank blocks (ebauchon) was placed that same month, and by the end of October, pipes made from them were being shipped to Paris, northern France, and Belgium. The testimony has never been confirmed by a second independent source; even so, it's frequently cited because it makes visible the distinction between "first trial" and "first commercial shipment."
Why No Single Name Emerges

Some claims point entirely outside Saint-Claude. In 1927, botanist and geographer Auguste Chevalier, stating that he did not adopt the information as his own view, published an account according to which the industry was born around 1850 in Saint-Paul-de-Fenouillet in the Eastern Pyrenees. A French book published in 1981 claims that the first rough briar pipes were whittled with a knife by Pyrenean peasants. Cogolin, in the Var, claims to have worked the burl of the Maures massif very early on; the town's specialization in high-quality pipe production, however, is dated in the records to around 1880. On a separate line, in 1986, American collector Richard C. Hacker claimed that manufacturer François Comoy, working in Saint-Claude, began carving briar around 1840; this date is more than a decade earlier than what other sources point to and isn't backed by any other record.

The community's present-day view is that searching for a single inventor is the wrong question. Tree heath may have fallen into the hands of many people around the Mediterranean basin, unbeknownst to one another; what mattered was not who first tried the material but that Saint-Claude, with its deep-rooted tradition of woodturning, rapidly turned it into an industry after 1855. The details of this transformation are covered in the article on the briar revolution.

r.x: The
Chicago Pipe Making Seminar Curriculum

is the written skeleton of the workshop course that has repeated for years as part of the international pipe show organized by the Chicagoland Pipe Collectors Club. The text is a curriculum outline showing which subjects the teaching team covers and in what order; in this sense it reads less as a single year's event announcement and more as a framework summarizing the topics hand pipe making is divided into.
The Framework of the Show and the Seminar

The club's show began in 1996, changed venues a few times within Illinois in its early years, and has, over time, come to be considered the world's most crowded pipe gathering. The making seminar is the longest-running part of the show's educational program outside the collector tables; in show announcements it's scheduled for the two days preceding the main days, and is advertised as a separate event requiring advance registration.

At the head of the course is Lee von Erck, a maker working in Michigan; it is often said that the seminar owes its present form to him, though the title of "founder" doesn't appear in independent records. The teaching staff changes from year to year: show announcements list names such as Michael Butera, Joe Nelson, and Andrew Petersen alongside von Erck. Records also show Jeff Gracik and Ernie Markle, who rose to instructor after going through the seminar himself, occasionally teaching as well, while Rex Poggenpohl is cited as an organizer on the administrative side. That the program defines separate staff for equipment setup and first aid shows that the machinery used in the workshop is meant to be taken seriously.
The Scope of the Practical Work

The material given to each participant is a pre-drilled briar block along with a vulcanite mouthpiece prepared to fit it; the blocks are covered by donated material. Since a single day isn't enough to make a pipe from scratch, the course focuses on the finishing stage. The goal isn't to train a master craftsman but to let the participant experience firsthand what hand pipe making consists of.
Course Topics

The rest of the program describes which topics a comprehensive course, one lasting longer than a single day, would need to cover. The framework opens with safety warnings and a brief history; how much the instructor will explain versus demonstrate is set up from the start as a balance to be struck.

The technical backbone is built on tying function to appearance. Bowl dimensions, the path of the smoke channel, condensation issues, and the mortise and tenon where the shank meets the mouthpiece are treated together as elements that both make a pipe smokeable and define its shape. On the material side, briar is introduced alongside mouthpiece materials (vulcanite and acrylic) and the materials used for shank extensions. The design discussion, meanwhile, sets classic French and English proportions against the freehand approach, which follows the direction of the grain.

Workshop tasks are also grouped under a few headings. Under drilling, there's a comparison of the drill press against the lathe, whether the holes should be drilled before or after shaping, and the choice of appropriate bits for the bowl and smoke channel. Shaping follows a sequence descending from coarse tools like sanding discs, belt sanders, knives, and files down to hand sanding. The finishing stage covers sandblasting, staining, bowl coating, stamping, and polishing; the difference between a single-tone finish and a two-tone contrast is also addressed separately. The program closes with the pouch and box that protect the pipe — that is, with presentation.

This framework shows that the seminar is not merely a hand-skills course: it introduces participants to a whole production chain running from design to presentation, all built around a single day's hands-on practice.

r.x: Morta

is oak wood at the earliest stage of fossilization, having lain buried in a peat bog or riverbed for thousands of years in an oxygen-free environment. It is also known as bog oak; in the Balkans it is called "abonos." Sources give varying ranges for how long it stays buried; typically wood aged between 2,000 and 6,000 years is cited. Alongside briar and meerschaum, it is a rare but well-regarded pipe bowl material thanks to its distinctive qualities.
Formation and Properties

The bog's acidic, oxygen-free environment protects the buried trunk from decay. During this long wait, the oak's tannins react with iron minerals in the water and the wood gradually darkens; black is the best-known color, though morta blocks in copper and gold tones also occur. This natural "leaching," spanning thousands of years, largely removes tannin, resin, and similar substances from the wood. For this reason morta is considered fully neutral in taste; the woody flavors briar can add to a smoke are absent in morta.

According to manufacturer data, mineral content that can exceed ten percent makes the bowl extraordinarily resistant to burning. Its porous, low-density structure absorbs moisture and condensation very well, which is why morta pipes are generally lightweight.
Working and Manufacturing

Morta is a demanding material for a pipe maker. The same block can hold soft and stone-hard regions side by side, and the rate of hidden flaws is high. Makers use tools in some steps that were designed for metal rather than wood. Because flaws often surface only at the final stage, dozens of hours of work can be lost; this high scrap rate is considered the main reason morta pipes are produced in small numbers, mostly by artisan makers. The block pulled from water must also be dried very slowly and under controlled conditions; rapid drying cracks the wood. The stages of making a pipe are similar for morta as for briar; the difference is that the material can surprise the maker at every step.

The main sources are Irish peat bogs and Balkan river basins; trunks pulled from the Sava basin in Croatia and Serbia in particular are well known. Trever Talbert and Davorin Denović are counted among the recognized makers who work with morta. Morta is also considered an environmentally friendly raw material: no new tree is cut, and trunks nature buried thousands of years ago are put to use instead.
Smoking Character and Care

Morta is known for giving a cool, dry, and slightly sweet smoke; its neutral structure reflects the tobacco's character as it is. This quality gives it value among smokers who want to taste blends without additional flavor. Like briar, it forms a cake inside the bowl; but because the body is brittle, keeping this layer thin is recommended.

Dry morta is hard but brittle; a dropped morta pipe cracks much more easily than briar does, so it should be protected carefully from impact. On the other hand, thanks to its high absorbency, resting between smokes is not considered as critical as it is with briar.
