r.x: The
clay pipe

is a pipe type, molded from white-firing pipe clay, in which bowl and stem form a single piece. From the late 16th century, when tobacco reached Europe, until the late 19th century, when cheap cigarettes spread, it remained the continent's near-universal pipe. Smoked everywhere from the tavern to the hearth, this cheap "people's pipe" went unrivaled among pipe bowl materials for roughly three centuries.
Making It and Its Smoking Character

In traditional production, white-firing pipe clay sourced from England or from around Cologne, Liège, and Rouen was hand-rolled into a fillet, the smoke channel opened with a thin wire, the body pressed in a greased metal mold, and the bowl shaped with a conical punch. Trimmed and stamped pipes were then fired at temperatures up to 1050°C. The heel stamps makers applied, along with the relief bowl decoration common between 1725 and 1825, served as the product's signature.

Clay's greatest virtue as a smoke is its neutrality: the material adds no flavor of its own to the tobacco and holds no ghost aroma, which is why tobacco blenders still use clay pipes for test smokes today. The bowl is also effectively burnout-proof; a dirtied pipe could simply be refired in an oven to clean it, and taverns even kept pipes hygienic by baking shared ones on iron grates. On the other hand the body heats up considerably (which is why a clay pipe is held by the stem rather than the bowl), the smoke runs hot and dry, and the pipe itself is extremely fragile. That's why millions of broken clay-pipe fragments turn up in the landfill and riverbed strata of European cities.
The Age of the Clay Pipe: From London to Gouda

The craft was born in England, around the 1580s and probably in London; the London pipe-makers' guild was founded in 1619. In England clay pipes were sold in dozen-count bundles and were often offered free to anyone buying tobacco at a tavern. The long-stemmed form that cooled the smoke went on to become a tradition of its own under the name churchwarden.

The craft was carried to continental Europe by the English who settled in the Dutch city of Gouda in the early 17th century; the two names most associated with this transfer are the English mercenaries said to have arrived in 1606, and William Baernelts, the English master who settled in the city in the years that followed and founded the first pipe workshop. By 1640 Gouda's output had overtaken England's; the pipe-makers' guild founded in the mid-17th century quickly grew to 180 members, and the first Gouda pipe fair was held in 1666. The peak came in the 18th century: 349 pipe workshops were counted in the city in 1749, and roughly half the population made its living from the trade.
A Different Path in the Ottoman World: Lüle

In the same centuries, the Ottoman world gave the clay pipe an entirely different form. In place of the single-piece, stemmed white European pipe, a stemless bowl — the lüle — was made from red clay and fitted onto the long wooden stem known as the çubuk (chibouk). The İstanbul center of this production was the Tophane district, which gave its name to the Tophane lüle tradition. The two traditions are considered two separate material cultures built around the same plant.
Decline and the Present Day

th-century, cheap cigarettes and briar pipes rapidly pushed the clay pipe out. Large Gouda manufacturers such as Goedewaagen and Zenith held on into the late 20th century; in the 1920s Zenith developed the double-walled bowl and the "doorroker" (mystery pipe) type, which revealed a glazed image underneath as it was smoked down. Today, clay-pipe making survives in Gouda through a handful of craftsmen; the craft was added to the Netherlands' intangible cultural heritage inventory in 2013. Broken pipe fragments, meanwhile, are a precise dating tool for archaeologists: stem-bore diameter, form typology, and maker's stamps are used to date 17th- to 19th-century strata.

r.x: This corncob pipe care guide

gathers the steps a smoker holding a new corncob can follow, from the first bowl to everyday maintenance. The material itself and its history are covered in the corncob pipe entry; the subject here is where a corncob behaves differently from a briar pipe, and the habits that difference calls for.
Checking Before the First Bowl

The bowl of a corncob pipe is the dried cob itself; the shank is fitted on separately afterward. Because production is machine-made, the fine craftsmanship expected of briar isn't expected here. Even so, it's worth checking two things before the first fill: whether the airway is clear and whether the end of the shank that extends into the bowl is smooth. Some Missouri Meerschaum models fit a hardwood plug into the bowl's base, considered an extra shield against burnout at the bottom. In versions without the plug, that role is largely taken over by the shank end that extends into the bowl, so removing that piece leaves the base unprotected.

Finished models get a plaster-based coating over the cob's exterior, topped with varnish; darker-looking versions also have color mixed into the coating. "Natural" versions carry no such layer at all, so polish or spray-type surface products are never applied to these pipes. Acrylic is the common stem material, and some models also accept a 6 mm filter.
Break-In and First Bowls

The long break-in routine applied to briar pipes isn't needed with corncob; the pipe can be filled and smoked the day it arrives. Still, in the first few bowls it's normal for the wooden shank end protruding into the bowl to char, and the flavor may not settle fully during this stage. The ash left behind by the charred piece fills the gaps around the base; the community generally holds that this buildup gradually turns into a thin insulating bed around the base.

Corncob smokers are split on the question of cake. One camp holds that the corncob's defining trait is that the bowl wall absorbs residue during a smoke and releases it back over time; a layer coating the wall cuts off that exchange and raises the risk of carrying one blend's flavor into the next — ghosting. The opposing camp maintains that a thin, regularly reamed layer protects the bowl from burning and smooths out the smoke. Both approaches have longtime corncob smokers behind them; the choice remains largely personal.
Cleaning, Moisture, and Lifespan

The manufacturer's care instructions call for wiping the bowl with a dry cloth after every smoke, removing the filter if present, and running a pipe cleaner through the shank. The alcohol and salt treatments common with briar bowls aren't recommended for corncob; because the material draws in liquid quickly, the structure can weaken. General cleaning steps are detailed in the pipe cleaning entry. The stem should not be removed until the pipe has fully cooled, and should be held by the shank rather than the bowl when removing it. Tapping the pipe against a hard surface to empty the ash can crack the bowl, so a light tap against the palm or a cork-tipped knocker is preferred. The manufacturer notes that the paper label on the bottom of the bowl also supports the structure and recommends against peeling it off.

The pipe's ability to absorb moisture and release it gradually calls for extra care in humid weather. A corncob pipe takes in not just the moisture from the tobacco but also the humidity of its surroundings, so it needs to fully dry out before refilling, just as it needs to cool. A corncob that is cleaned regularly and rested adequately between smokes is reported to give many years of service.

r.x: Pipe making

is the handcraft in which every stage of a pipe, from the rough block to the finished product, is carried out by a single person. In a factory the work is divided among many stations, each tied to its own machine; this arrangement is described in the how a pipe is made entry. At workshop scale, every decision — from which grain in the block will stand out to the diameter of the airway — falls to the same person. The craft has no written curriculum; knowledge builds up largely through trial and error and through practical solutions makers pass on to one another.
Block and Stem Material

The briar burl used for the body (stummel) is dug up between thirty and sixty years of age; details are in the briar entry. Two different cuts come out of a burl. "Ebauchon" blocks, cut from the interior, are more plentiful and cheaper, but are considered more likely to contain a crack or void inside. "Plateaux" blocks, cut from the outer surface, are considered superior in grain pattern and are the preference of most craftsmen.

The stem, meanwhile, is worked from rod-form material. Of the two common options, ebonite is a hard rubber obtained by long vulcanization of natural rubber with sulfur and linseed oil; its sulfur content ranges from 25 to 80 percent. Ultraviolet light oxidizes the surface over time, after which free sulfur bonds with moisture to form sulfate and sulfuric acid; the surface gradually shifts from grayish green to brown. Acrylic does not show this degradation. The two are compared in the stem materials entry.
The Body's Internal Dimensions

Turning the block into a pipe depends on opening three separate holes: the chamber where the tobacco burns, the draught hole that carries smoke along the shank, and the mortise where the stem sits. Their placement in the pipe is shown in the pipe anatomy entry. The measurements cited in workshop circles are not a binding standard but a debated range: roughly 16-25 mm for chamber diameter, 3.2-4.3 mm for the draught hole, and 6-9.5 mm for the mortise, with figures around 8 mm considered customary for the mortise. The airway's effect on smoking is debated constantly among makers; alongside diameter, keeping the cross-sectional volume constant along the shank is also considered decisive.

At what stage the holes are drilled varies from workshop to workshop. The common approach is to drill the holes while the block is still rough and build the shape around those axes. The reverse is also practiced: when the body is shaped first and the holes drilled afterward, the line where the grain looks best and the flaws are minimized can be chosen — but since there's no margin for correction left, a single wrongly drilled hole ruins the block. This second approach is said to be preferred in circles around the Danish school.
Stem and Tenon

Ready-molded stems come in a limited number of shapes and sizes; they need to be filed down before fitting to the shank, and heated and bent for curved bodies. In hand-cut work, the stem is shaped from rod material starting from scratch, specifically for that one body; with the mold constraint removed, body and stem become part of the same design.

The tenon connecting the stem to the shank is either turned from the stem's own material or glued on as a separate piece. In the second approach, a widely used material is the acetal resin (polyoxymethylene, POM) marketed by DuPont as Delrin. Its coefficient of friction is low, it's wear-resistant, and its dimensional stability is high; it can withstand continuous use up to 80 °C. Its self-lubricating surface allows the stem to be removed and reinserted frequently. Its very sturdiness also has a downside: if the pipe is dropped, the shank is more likely to break than the tenon, and shank repair is far more difficult than stem repair.
Getting Started with a Pipe Kit

Because drilling mistakes can't be undone, most beginners start out with ready-made sets — a "pipe kit" — whose body is already drilled and stem roughly fitted. In these sets, what's left to the maker is shaping, sanding, and polishing. Kits are prepared separately for straight, bent, and freehand bodies; the stem connection can be flush or military-mount.

The equipment needed to finish a kit is modest: a variable-speed hand drill, a flexible sanding disc, files in various cuts, a coping saw for rough shaping, buffing wheels, and carnauba wax. Because wood dust irritates the airways, safety glasses and a dust mask are considered mandatory. Once work moves to drilling the block itself, the list expands to include a drill press or lathe, chamber bits, and fine drill bits for the airway.

r.x: Shell Briar and Tanshell patent stamps

are among the most reliable ways to date Dunhill's sandblasted pipes across a span of roughly forty years. The sandblasting method, registered in 1917, and the earlier-dated inner-tube invention, were stamped side by side on the same pipe for a long time. If you know which country a number belongs to and over what span it was used, you can roughly read which decade a body dates from.
Two Separate Inventions, One Stamp Cluster

The inner tube is a thin aluminum tube running through the shank; it prevents the airway from clogging by collecting tar. Records indicate this device was registered in 1912; on pipes it appears as number 5861/12. Sandblasting's registration year is 1917, though the stamp was used on pipes only from 1918 on, reading as 119708/17. For this reason, early sandblast examples often carry both numbers together. For the method's place in the brand's history, see the History of Dunhill's Shell Briar entry.
Periods of the Numbers
The ranges below summarize the combinations most often cited in stamp catalogs.

Published lists note that number 1861910/32 also appears on some bodies bound for the American market between 1932 and 1934. Number 15114/34, used briefly between 1934 and 1935, is a provisional registration. For corrections on Canadian numbers, the A Correction on Canadian Patents entry is useful.
Points to Watch When Reading

The two digits after the slash are the patent's registration year; the year the stamp actually started being used on a pipe is often one or two years later. Also, under the year-code system introduced in 1921, a small digit was added after the patent number (on some bodies after the word ENGLAND); though it took until the following year to become widespread, this addition gives a more precise result than the patent range alone. For a detailed table, see the Dunhill Patent Stamps and Dating entry.

After 1954, once patent stamps fell out of use, dating relies entirely on year suffixes and finish names. In this period the brand's sandblasted line split in two: the dark-colored Shell Briar and the light brown Tanshell, introduced in 1952. The small number of Tanshell examples made in the first year are considered experimental, said to use Algerian briar, with the harder, denser Sardinian briar becoming standard from 1953 on. For the brand's general framework, see the Dunhill (White Spot) entry.

r.x: Shaping on a lathe

is the process of mounting a roughly cut briar block on a wood lathe and turning it, around its axis of rotation, into a symmetrical body. In pipe making the lathe is used not just for drilling holes but also for forming the round surfaces of the bowl's exterior and the shank. It's considered the most direct way to hit the standard proportions of the round-sectioned classic shapes, especially the billiard family. The process is a basic stage both in mass-production workshops and at the benches of makers who craft pipes one at a time; the difference mostly lies in where the lathe leaves off and hand work takes over.
Working with an Unbalanced Piece

The whole technical difficulty of shaping on a lathe stems from one fact: a briar block is irregular in its natural form, and once mounted on the machine its center of mass almost never coincides with the axis of rotation. The resulting wobble not only leaves ripples on the surface, it also constantly stresses the mounting point. Practical solutions cluster around this single problem.

The first is mass. A heavy-bodied wood lathe absorbs the wobble; a light machine amplifies vibration in the same piece. Second is the reliability of the mount: the chuck's jaws are given as wide a gripping boss on the block as possible, since the greater the contact surface, the lower the chance of the piece slipping from the grip. Third is the state of the tool; a dulled edge tears the fiber instead of cutting it, leaving marks whose correction is left to the sanding stage.
Speed and Cutting Order

Speed selection also ties back to this same imbalance issue. Established practice is to work at low speed while the piece is still rough and wobbly, and to raise the speed gradually as the shape rounds out and balances around the mass axis; higher speed gives a cleaner cutting surface once the right conditions are in place. A specific upper-limit figure isn't a measured value particular to pipe making and varies by machine, block size, and chuck. In every case the tool should rest firmly on the tool rest, with the cutting point kept close to the axis.

Workshops split on the order of operations. Some makers drill the holes first and shape the block around that axis; others follow the shape-first, drill-later path. In either case, if the piece mounted on the lathe can be carried into lathe drilling and tenon turning without breaking the same mount, axis misalignment is minimized.
The Lathe's Limit

What the machine can deliver is, by definition, a surface symmetrical around the axis of rotation. This limits the lathe to a certain family of shapes: circular-sectioned bowls, straight and tapered shanks, band seats. The lathe only produces surfaces of revolution. In freehand work chasing the point where the grain looks most striking, with flattened cheeks or asymmetrical bowl mouths, the machine only takes you so far; the rest is belt sander, file, and hand work. This is why experienced makers treat the lathe as a roughing tool that quickly reduces the amount of material to be removed from a briar block, and make their finishing decisions only after taking the piece off the machine.

r.x: Reading a sandblasted surface

means seeing that the relief on a stummel isn't a pattern applied for decoration, but the exposed structure of the wood itself. Sandblasting doesn't add a new form to the surface; it makes tangible the difference between the wood's hard and soft zones. That's why two pipes put through the same process are never identical, and even the two sides of a single stummel can turn out different.
What the Rings Say

Every growing season leaves a ring in tree heath's root burl; as a rule, one ring corresponds to one year. The early wood formed at the start of the season is the product of fast growth — loose and soft; the late wood forming toward the season's end is denser and harder. Pressurized abrasive doesn't treat these two textures alike: the soft one wears away quickly, the hard one resists, leaving behind ridges stacked back to back. Ring width isn't constant either; a wet, long season leaves a wide ring, a dry year a narrow one. Briar burls are mostly harvested between thirty and sixty years of age, so a single stummel can show tight and loose ring clusters side by side.
The Surface Reveals the Block's Orientation

While rings stack layer by layer within the burl, grain lines are fibers running crosswise through those layers. What shows on the surface depends on how these two systems are oriented relative to the bowl. When the fibers are cut from the side, the layers are exposed one by one and distinct ridges read across the stummel. When the fiber ends face the surface instead, there are no rings left to read — the layers are being viewed not from the side but from above — and the mottled texture called birdseye appears. Because the grain fans out around the bowl, one side of a stummel can be ridged while the other is mottled. The rings running flat or at an angle along the length of the stummel comes from the same structure: when the bowl's axis meets the layers at a right angle, the rings read like a stack piled one on top of another; when the axis meets the layers at an angle, the bands instead lie lengthwise along the stummel.
The Limit of Depth

As reported from maker observation, how deep the abrasive can dig between layers is largely governed by how tight the grain fibers are: the tighter the fibers, the more they support each other, and the shallower the surface stays. This explains why blocks with the very tightest grain — the most prized for a smooth finish — often produce dull, low-relief blasts, while deep, rugged surfaces tend to come from comparatively looser-grained wood. It's also said that raising pressure has a ceiling of its own; past a certain point, instead of the relief deepening further, the whole surface drops together. The shallowness of the birdseye zone is attributed to the same framework. These are bench-derived criteria rather than topics treated directly in wood-anatomy literature.
Source of the Criterion

One known text laying out this way of reading from a maker's own eye is the article Talbert Pipes co-founder Trever Talbert published in his workshop journal on 10 May 2008. The text's conclusion is plain: the difference in texture between two sides more often comes from the wood's orientation than from the application. Such a reading doesn't declare one surface finish good or bad; it only helps name what's being looked at correctly.

r.x: The bamboo shank

is the construction of the section between a pipe's bowl and its mouthpiece using a jointed segment cut from a bamboo stalk instead of wood. The bowl is usually made from briar, but the shank is left short; bamboo completes the remaining distance. Because the rings the nodes leave on the piece determine the pipe's appearance, the bamboo shank is a choice of both construction and form.
What the Material Provides

A bamboo stalk is a hollow tube between nodes; this natural cavity offers a ready-made axis to follow when drilling the smoke channel. The material's density is also low: when the briar shank is shortened and bamboo takes its place, the pipe's total weight drops noticeably. This is the main reason the bamboo shank is favored among smokers who carry the pipe in their teeth. Bamboo's moisture absorption is often cited in the community as a reason for a drier smoke; this should be taken as a widely held view rather than a measured figure.

The distance between nodes and the number of nodes determine the shank's character. For a long time two- or three-node pieces were accepted as the standard; as suppliers' cutting habits changed, four- and five-node pieces also reached workshops from the mid-2000s onward. The small root protrusions left at the nodes are either sanded flat or hollowed out and filled with resin; the second route also seals that point against moisture.
Its Roots in the East and Its Passage to the West

Bamboo's place in Asian smoking implements is old. In the "rau" type of the Japanese kiseru pipe, the intermediate tube between the mouthpiece (suikuchi) and the metal bowl-and-neck piece (gankubi) is made of bamboo; the type takes its name from this section. The known early example in Western pipe making is the bamboo-shanked models Dunhill catalogued under the name Whangee. It is noted that this name refers to a species of bamboo in Chinese and had been used earlier in the cane and umbrella-handle trade. Sources diverge on the line's beginning: some accounts point to the 1920s, others to the period after the Second World War when briar was scarce; what is certain is that the model appears in the 1951 catalogue. Stanwell is reported to have used bamboo starting in the early 1950s. The maker generally credited as the first to treat bamboo not as a fix for a shortage but as a deliberate design element is Sixten Ivarsson. Today the bamboo shank sits in the repertoire of a wide circle of makers, from Denmark to Japan to America.
Two Joints Built in the Workshop

Because the bamboo shank is a third piece inserted between the bowl and the mouthpiece, it presents the maker with two joints instead of one. The technical core of the work is resolving these two connections. At the start of preparation, the piece is thoroughly dried, then bored end to end following the natural cavity between nodes; the boring is mostly done on the lathe, and the two ends are flattened perpendicular to the channel so that the joining surfaces sit without gaps.

On the bowl side of the connection, a stainless-steel tube is passed into the bamboo; the tube both aligns the two holes on the same axis and widens the bonding surface, making the joint load-bearing. On the mouthpiece side, a wider socket is opened and a Delrin rod is set into it. This way, the surface the tenon rubs against is not bamboo but hard plastic; this is what absorbs wear at a joint that is frequently taken apart and reassembled. Fitting thin ebonite rings at both ends is a common practice: the ring softens the color and texture difference as it moves from briar to bamboo and from bamboo to the mouthpiece. A comparison of mouthpiece materials is in the mouthpiece materials entry.

In terms of sequence, the bowl's shape is largely finished before the bamboo is glued on; a flaw emerging late from within the wood would take the already-prepared bamboo down with it at that stage. In this construction, since no separate socket is opened for the mouthpiece, the mouthpiece's angle stays tied to that of the smoke channel, narrowing the range of angles left to the maker's discretion.

r.x: BriarWorks

is an American manufacturing venture founded in Tennessee by pipe makers Todd Johnson and Pete Prevost, aimed at combining mass production with workshop craftsmanship. What sets the brand apart from its peers is less its products than its production setup: the lathes that shape its pipes weren't bought ready-made — they were designed and built in-house, within the workshop itself. Almost everything known about the founding process rests on Johnson's own account, shared on a maker forum and passed on to Pipedia before 2015; since it has no counterpart in independent records, the details below are given based on that account.
The Lathe Before the Pipe

According to Johnson's account, the founders' first obstacle was that no machine park existed on the market capable of turning out shapes considered unusual for factory-produced pipes. The needed lathes were first commissioned from an outside firm, and when the work delivered after roughly six months wasn't deemed adequate, the pair took the job on themselves. What made this decision possible was that Johnson had spent years building custom cars and motorcycles, and Prevost had a background in welding. According to the same account, the first lathes were welded together over two and a half months, starting from hand-drawn sketches, and production began after the prototyping and testing period that followed. Four more lathes were added in subsequent years, with each new machine's design revisited in light of the ones before it; at the time the account was written, monthly production was said to be around two thousand units.
Walking Away from China

The venture actually began on another continent. According to Johnson's telling, the original plan was a factory set up in China to produce pipes for the Chinese market; after roughly a year and a half of back-and-forth, it became clear that production only reached the desired standard when he was physically present at the facility. That left two options: move the family there to live for a while, or accept whatever came out of the factory in his absence. With preparations for the move well underway, the plan was abandoned altogether, and the decision was made to set up production in the United States instead. The workshop's founding in Tennessee is the result of that reversal.
Its Place in the Definitional Debate

The BriarWorks example is often cited in discussions of the handmade versus machine-made distinction. The rough shape is cut on a lathe; on the other hand, the lathes themselves weren't bought ready-made but built in-house, and every step after that is finished by hand. The question of at what threshold a production run counts as "handmade" also shows why the line between artisan pipes and factory pipes resists a settled definition.
From Workshop to Brand

The rough shape coming off the lathe is finished by hand by the team; sanding, staining, buffing, chamber lining, and stamping are all done at this stage. The workshop has also stayed open to training new makers, teaching the fundamentals through short-term work and learning programs. The staff later grew with the addition of well-known carvers such as Bill Shalosky and Micah Redmond.

The brand today runs a line based on the classic shape chart, its own in-house designs, and a single calabash shape, as separate ranges; the plainer-crafted Moonshine line also comes out of the same workshop. Production started in Nashville and later moved to Columbia, also in Tennessee. After Johnson left the workshop, Pete Prevost has headed the operation. For the brand's product range and stamping conventions, see the BriarWorks entry; for the material used itself, see the briar entry.

r.x: Briar pipe shape names

are not a classification defined by any central body but a vocabulary that settled by itself out of the everyday language of catalogues, trade journals, and the shop counter. Three distinct layers sit intertwined within this vocabulary: names pointing to an actual person or place, names directly describing the shape, and historical coincidences that no longer have a visual counterpart today. Why the repertoire of classic pipe shapes looks so inconsistent is explained largely by these three layers blending into one another.
Names from People and Places

Lovat is traced to the title Lord Lovat, which reaches back to the 15th century in Scottish nobility; it is associated in particular with Simon Joseph Fraser, 23rd Chief of Clan Fraser of Lovat and a lieutenant general, who lived from 1871 to 1933. Oom Paul means "Uncle Paul" in Afrikaans and was the nickname of Stephanus Johannes Paulus Kruger (1825-1904), who served as president of the South African Republic (Transvaal) from 1883 to 1900; Kruger is remembered in English sources of the period together with his pipe.

Prince is credited to Edward VII, who was born Albert Edward and was known as the Prince of Wales from 1841 to 1901; the king was a known heavy tobacco user. Which firm designed the shape is disputed, and the often-repeated Dunhill attribution is not certain. In fact, the firm's first royal warrant, granted in 1921, came not from Edward VII but from a later Edward who was then Prince of Wales. Place-based naming is older still: the Dublin shape is understood to take its name from the city, and in the clay pipe era naming a pipe after the town where it was made was already standard practice.
Names That Don't Keep Their Promise, and Names Abandoned

Not every name points to what it promises. Canadian has no established connection to Canada, nor does Belge (Belgique) to Belgium; Canadian today describes a family defined not by the country but by its long, flattened shank, gathered under the heading of the Canadian family.
Some names have fallen out of use altogether. The starkest example is the term "kaffir," recorded as appearing in Kapp & Peterson catalogues in the early 20th century. Derived from the Arabic word
kafir

, the term had, by the mid-20th century, become a severe racial slur in South Africa and was brought within the scope of hate speech legislation by a law passed in 2000. Peterson subsequently referred to the same shape under names such as Zulu, Woodstock, or Yachtsman. A quieter disappearance is the name Unger (also recorded as Ungar): although it was listed among the "standard" shapes in American sales guides from 1919 and 1922, it appears in almost no catalogue today.
From Abundance to Numbers

By the end of the century, there was no rule constraining manufacturers in how they named things. An 1896 English trade journal ties the practice of giving briar shapes flashy names like Chubby, Tourist, Regent, and Midget to a thoroughly practical reason: so that a customer who liked a pipe could reorder it by name. New names were added rapidly. In 1908, Rhodesian, Pan, and Calabash were announced as new entries to the industry; by 1913, a well-known firm's catalogue was reported to list one hundred fifty separate shapes.

This abundance created its own problem. According to a 1918 report, the William Demuth firm reduced the number of shapes on a single production line to twenty-four. Sales guides from those same years list only a handful of shapes, such as straight and bent bulldog and egg, under a "standard" heading. By 1922, Dunhill's New York representative had abandoned naming altogether: every shape was given a number, and the customer was shown to the drawer that matched it. This is the origin of why name and number still coexist today in briar pipes. The name carries the story; the number carries the measurement.

r.x: A
Delrin tenon

is a joint formed by preparing the projection that seats the mouthpiece into the shank from a separate acetal rod and gluing it into the mouthpiece, rather than turning it from the mouthpiece material itself. Delrin is DuPont's trade name for its polyoxymethylene (POM)-based acetal resin; the resin is on record as having entered mass production in 1960. The material's arrival at the pipe bench is much more recent, and its rationale is not aesthetic but entirely practical.
The Logic of a Separate Tenon

With a tenon turned from the mouthpiece itself, the diameter is left to the maker's hand and the lathe's setting each time; with a ready-made rod, the diameter is known from the start. Because acetal is manufactured to tight tolerances, every rod of a given size is, in practice, the same diameter, so the fit becomes repeatable from pipe to pipe. The second gain is on the repair side: a broken acetal tenon can be removed and replaced with a new one without sacrificing the mouthpiece itself.

There's no binding standard for diameter selection; workshop habit is what decides. A 5/16-inch (roughly 8 mm) rod is most often preferred; 1/4- and 3/8-inch sizes are also used. The decision is made according to the final thickness of the mouthpiece and shank.
Two Faces of Acetal

Two behaviors make the material suitable for this job. The first is dimensional stability: because the piece holds its size under heat and pressure, it doesn't drift while being drilled. The second is its low friction and the accompanying self-lubricating behavior; the mouthpiece slides in and out of the mortise smoothly, without squeaking.

The same slipperiness exacts its price at assembly. POM is among the materials most resistant to adhesive; the bond forms not chemically but mechanically. In practice, this means cutting a groove around the area to be glued, then deepening these grooves further with a file at three points around the circumference. Once the epoxy cures, these irregularities form a lock that keeps the rod from spinning within the mortise.
A Fixed Rod, a Variable Hole

The hard part of the job isn't the rod but the hole meant to receive it; while the rod arrives at a fixed size, the hole is affected by three factors. The first is the drill bit: bits stamped with the same size can give different actual diameters from brand to brand, so a maker has to test the bit they're going to use in advance and set aside the ones that have worked. The second is the material. Testing must always be done on briar pieces, because other woods don't react the same way when drilled and can give a misleading result; in vulcanite and acrylic, meanwhile, the bit that gives a correct fit in briar often runs too tight, so separate bits may be needed for the body and the mouthpiece. These differences among mouthpiece materials are covered separately in the article on mouthpiece materials. The third is drilling technique: because heat and pressure from chips accumulating in the mortise can change the final diameter, the bit is fully withdrawn and cleared at short intervals.
From Gluing to Final Fitting

The bottom of the mortise drilled into the mouthpiece is left flat, and the end of the rod is prepared to match this bottom; the aim is to minimize any gaps where epoxy could pool. The resin is applied to both surfaces in a thin, even layer, the pieces are pressed together and rotated to release air bubbles, and any excess epoxy is wiped away before it cures. Drilling or taking measurements is not attempted before the cure is complete; fast-curing resins shorten the working time but reach full strength later.

Two approaches are followed for opening the smoke channel. Some makers drill the channel while the rod is still separate; others glue the rod to the mouthpiece first and then drill both together, without removing the piece from the lathe. The second route is often recommended because it reduces the risk of misalignment; the bench-side details are described in the article on drilling on the lathe. In the final stage, the tenon is shortened to match the depth of the mortise in the body, and its end is lightly chamfered so it doesn't score the mortise. How a fit that has loosened or tightened over time is adjusted is covered in the article on pipe repair and mouthpiece maintenance.
